MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED LEGISLATION
Sub-clause ( 1) of clause 5 of the Bill confers power upon the Central
Government to issue orders to specify the organisation referred to in the clause
as an organisation of a political nature not being a political party referred to in
clause 3( 1).
2. Clause 48 of the Bill confers power upon the Central Government to
make rules for carrying out the provisions of the proposed legislation. The matters
in respect of which rules may be made relate, inter alia , to, the value of the article
and the authority which may be specified under clause 2( 1); acceptance or
retention of gift or presentation under clause 4; ground or grounds on which an
organisation may be specified as an organisation of political nature under clause
5(2); the manner in which the administrative expenses shall be calculated under
clause 8( 2); the time within which and manner in which any person or class of
persons or an association may be required to furnish intimation regarding the
amount of foreign contribution received under clause 9; the time within which and
manner in which any person or class of persons may be required to furnish
intimation regarding foreign hospitality under clause 9; the manner in which the
copy of the order of the Central Government shall be served upon any person
under clause 10; the form and manner in which the application for grant of
certificate of registration on giving of prior permission and fee therefor under
clause 12( 1); the terms and conditions for granting a certificate or giving prior
permission under clause 12( 3); the manner of utilising the foreign contribution
under clause 13( 2); the authority with whom the foreign contribution to be vested
under clause 15( 1); the period within which and the manner in which the foreign
contribution shall be managed under clause 15( 2); the form and manner in which
the application for renewal of certificate of registration shall be made and the fees
therefor under clause 16( 2); the form and manner in which the foreign remittance
received in any of the accounts of the bank or authorised person in foreign
exchange which shall be reported under clause 17( 2); the time within which and
the manner in which the person who has been granted certificate of registration
or given prior permission shall give intimation under clause 18; the form and
manner in which account of any foreign contribution and the manner in which
such contribution has been utilised shall be maintained under clause 19; the time
within which and manner in which a candidate for election shall give intimation
under clause 21; the manner and procedure to be followed in disposing of the
assets under clause 22; the limits subject to which any confiscation may be
adjudged under clause 29( 1); the fee to be accompanied along with every
application for revision under clause 32( 5); the form and manner for making of
an application for compounding of an offence and the fees therefor under clause
41(4); the form and manner in which and the time within which returns and
statements to be furnished by the prescribed authority under clause 44; any other
matter which is required to be, or may be, prescribed.
3. The matters in respect of which orders may be issued and the rules
may be made by the Central Government are generally matters of procedure and
administrative detail and it is not practicable to provide for them in the Bill itself.
The delegation of legislative power is, therefore, of a normal character.

PREFACE
I, the Chairperson of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home
Affairs, having been authorized by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred and Thirty-fifth Report on Border Fencing and Floodlighting Projects of
Indo-Pak Border pertaining to the Ministry of Home Affairs.
2. The Sub-Committee on Border Fencing and Floodlighting Projects of the Department-related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs was constituted on 13th April, 2007 for in-
depth examination of the Border Fencing and Floodlighting Projects. The Sub-Committee was
reconstituted on 9th August, 2007.
3. The Sub-Committee heard the presentation of the representatives of Ministry of Home
Affairs on 1st June, 2007. The Secretary, Border Management gave a detailed account of various
activities being undertaken by the Government under the border fencing and floodlighting projects.
4. The Sub-Committee held five sittings and undertook study visits to border areas of
Rajasthan, Gujarat, Jammu and Kashmir and Punjab. As decided by the Sub-Committee in its
meeting held on 1st June, 2007, it has restricted itself to the Indo-Pak border in the current study.
5. During the on-the-spot study visit to border areas of Rajasthan and Gujarat, certain issues
concerning the implementation of the project were brought to the notice of the Sub-Committee.
The Sub-Committee heard the views of the representatives of BSF and CPWD in its meeting held
on 22nd October, 2007. The Sub-Committee was informed that the Gujarat Sector of Indo-Pak
Border suffered from geo-climatic disadvantages for border fencing and floodlighting. This sector
had faced disastrous earthquake in Bhuj area in 2001 followed by flood in 2003. The area had also
received unprecedented downpour in 2006-07 which led to the cost and time overrun of the
project. The marshy land with high degree of salinity derailed the project of Border Fencing.
Moreover, ban on mining of stones and sand by the State Government further delayed the projects
in the Sector as the material had to be carted from Rajasthan. The Sub-Committee was also
informed that due to non-release of funds in time, the construction work had come to a standstill.
6. The Sub-Committee was further informed that the final anticipated revised cost of the
project stood of Rs. 1210 crore. Sanction for the upgradation works and approval of the revised
estimates were awaited since August, 2007. The project required CCS approval for the revised cost
of Rs. 1210 crore for border works in the Gujarat Sector. The Convenor of the Sub-Committee
in his letter dated 25 October, 2007 brought all these facts to the notice of the Home Minister and
requested him that appropriate funds, as per the revised estimate, be released for completion of the
project in time.
7. In its meetings held on 30th November, 2007 and 6th May, 2008 the Sub-Committee held
internal discussions on the subject. The Convenor of the Sub-Committee submitted the report to
the main Committee for consideration and adoption.
8. The Committee in its sitting held on 3rd October, 2008 considered and adopted the report.
SUSHMA SWARAJ

1
REPORT
CHAPTER-I
OVERVIEW OF BORDER AREAS
1.1 The Sub-Committee was apprised by the Ministry of Home Affairs that the necessity for
border fencing and floodlighting arose primarily because of the fact that the border areas of the
country specially Indo Bangladesh and Indo-Pak borders were vulnerable to infiltration and various
type of illegal activities from across the border which were prejudicial to the interest of the nation.
As the physical patrolling of the areas had not proved adequate to stop such activities along the
long stretch of the border, border fencing and floodlighting projects had been chalked out as a
mechanism to control such infiltration and cross border illegal activities.
1.2 The Ministry of Home Affairs informed the Sub-Committee that Punjab Action Plan (PAP)
was chalked out to counter the insurgency activities in the State, including measures for more
effective policing of the border, better intelligence gathering, concerted action to check smuggling,
better policing of the villages and an integrated approach for development of border districts.
Punjab Action Plan included fencing and floodlighting of the border, electronic surveillance and
laying of jeepable tracks etc. Subsequently, the Government also approved proposals for fencing
and floodlighting the Rajasthan, Gujarat and the Jammu international borders.
1.3 The details of the fencing and floodlighting projects including other aspects, as furnished
by the Ministry of Home Affairs in their background note and during the meetings of the sub-
Committee, are given in the succeeding paragraphs.
Punjab Action Plan
1.4.1 The Ministry has stated that in 1988, a Punjab Action Plan was prepared to counter the
insurgent activities in Punjab. Various working groups were constituted to deal with manpower,
technology, cost, time-schedule and all other aspects required to implement PAP. Subsequently on
20th April, 1988 High Level Empowered Committee (HLEC) was constituted, under the
chairmanship of Home Secretary, to take various measures, including fencing and floodlighting on
Indo-Pak border.
1.4.2 In Punjab, fencing/floodlighting works were started in May, 1988 and completed in
November, 1993. A total length of 461 km had been fenced and floodlit in the entire Punjab sector,
at a total cost of Rs. 147.65 crore. It was stated that as a result of fencing/floodlighting of the
Punjab sector, terrorism and other anti-national activities from across the border have been checked
to a large extent. Fencing/floodlighting in this sector is maintained by BSF.
Rajasthan Border
1.5.1 A total length of 1048 kms. of fencing and 1023 km floodlighting in the Rajasthan sector
was completed in the year 1999 at a cost of Rs. 401.64 crore. 275 Kms. of border roads have
also been constructed on Rajasthan border to facilitate patrolling by BSF. It was stated that as a
result of fencing/floodlighting of the Rajasthan sector, terrorism and other anti-national activities
from across the border had been checked to a large extent. The fencing and floodlighting in this
sector is also maintained by BSF.

2
Gujarat Border
1.6.1 The Indo-Pak border in Gujarat extends from the mouth of Sir Creek to the tri-junction of
the Mavasari in Banaskantha District (Gujarat) and Bakasur in Barmer District (Rajasthan) (a length
of 508 km); and is known as Rann of Kutch, comprising Great Rann and Little Rann. It is bounded
in the South by the Gulf of Kutch, in the West by Indian Ocean and in the North-East and South-
East by the Districts of Banaskantha, Mehsana and Kutch.
1.6.2 The border areas of Gujarat and Rann are sparsely inhabited and the harsh climate poses
many problems to the troops in manning it effectively. BSF Border Out Posts are situated 20 to
50 kms. inward from the International Border. The terrain is non-negotiable during the monsoon
and post-monsoon seasons. As a result, proper border vigil is not possible and the area is
increasingly exploited by the smugglers/ISI agents for their nefarious activities. The Ministry stated
that to prevent the exploitation of the Gujarat border by anti-national elements, BSF had proposed
construction of fencing, floodlighting and border roads in the feasible stretches in the Gujarat
sector of Indo-Pak border to facilitate forward shift of the BSF Posts towards the International
Border. This proposal was approved, in principle, by High Level Empowered Committee (HLEC)
in its meeting held on 8th January, 1997 and it was decided that a suitable design, taking into
consideration the physical conditions (on account of the area becoming marshy during rainy
season), should jointly be evolved by BSF and CPWD.
1.6.3 It was further stated that in order to check illegal activities, Government approved a
comprehensive proposal for construction of fencing/floodlighting on raised embankment,
construction of link roads, BOPs and border roads at an estimated cost of Rs. 380 crore on the
Gujarat border. A total length of 310 km. of fencing and floodlighting was approved. Out of this,
215 Km. of fencing was allocated to CPWD and 95 km to NBCC. Out of this, fencing on a stretch
of 217 km. and floodlighting on 178 km. had been completed as on 31st March, 2007. The
fencing is done by CPWD and NBCC and floodlighting by CPWD. The remaining work is under
progress. The fencing and floodlighting work in Gujarat was earlier targeted to be completed by
31st March, 2007. It was stated that the targets could not be achieved due to unprecedented rains
in Gujarat during the year 2006.
1.6.4 The sub-Committee was informed that as a result of fencing/floodlighting of the Gujarat
sector, terrorism and other anti-national activities from across the border had been checked to a
large extent. The fencing and floodlighting work in this sector is maintained by CPWD.
Jammu International Border

CHAPTER-II
ON-THE-SPOT STUDY OF BORDER AREAS OF RAJASTHAN AND GUJARAT
2.1 The Sub-Committee visited Jaisalmer and Barmer sectors on 29th and 30th June, 2007.
During its visit, the following issues came up for special mention:—
• SHQ BSF Jaisalmer is one of the largest sectors having an area of responsibility of
470 kms., with some Battalions for taking care of 122 BOPs and 187 gates.
• The areas in Pakistan opposite to the Jaisalmer sector are Bahawalpur, Rahimyar Khan,
Ghotki, Sukkur and Khairpur Mir. The areas opposite to Barmer Sector are Khairpur,
Sanghar, Umarkot and Mithi Distts. of Sindh province.
• The terrain is generally sandy with permanent and shifting sand dunes of varying
height of 10 to 50 metres.
• There was scarcity of water and water support system extends from 45 to 150 Kms.
• The personnel posted there are vulnerable to some of the health hazards like sunstroke,
dehydration, death due to snake-bite, water prone diseases, vision problem and
breathing problems due to duststorm.
• Length of double fencing with Border Fencing Light (BFL) is 437.5 Kms. and Length
of experimental single fencing (with BFL) in shifting sand area is 6.5 Kms. A length
of 26 Kms. in 5 stretches for construction of single fencing (with BFL) is underway.
• Single Fence was not successful and was mostly damaged/buried/uprooted/tilted due to
shifting sand dunes. However, experimental fencing done in 6.5 kms. has been
successful even after three summers and based on this success, fencing work of 26
kms. is being undertaken. Proposal for lighting of 26 Kms. border area is under
submission.
• Crime, smuggling of drugs, gold, silver were rampant. However, with the erection of
fencing, floodlighting and forward shifting of BOPs in 1996, the smuggling had come
down to zero level.
• Besides routine patrolling, zero line patrolling is also done by each BOP once a week.
• Four types of tracks namely (i) Zero line track, (ii) Fencing track, (iii) Gypsy track,
(vi) Adm track are maintained meticulously as there is no metal/gravel road.
• The sector is organizing events which are aimed to promote a sense of mutual
cooperation, trust, goodwill and coordination with local community and thereby
enhancing the image of BSF among local population. Various civic action programmes
like medical camps, blood donation camp, pulse polio camp and distribution of
educational material in border villages were also undertaken.
2.2 The following issues were placed before the sub-Committee for immediate consideration:
• Lateral and Axial Roads upto the BOPs may be constructed to enhance the operational
efficiency.
4

5
• One tractor may be provided to each company for maintenance of border tracks.
• There is scarcity of water for use of BSF Personnel, tree-plantation and wildlife along
BOP line. A water pipe line needs to be provided.
• Opening of Kendriya Vidyalaya may be expedited.
• Desert/remote areas allowance and ration money may be granted.
• Leave of BSF personnel maybe granted sympathetically.
• Operational problems, as one Battalion is entrusted on an average with the task of
manning 60-62 kms., which proves not only arduous but sometimes unmanageable.
Observations/Recommendations
2.3.1 The Committee hails the stellar role of BSF in guarding the country’s frontiers
under tremendous adverse circumstances due to geographical, climatic and other conditions.
Our borders are secure due to their diligence, loyalty and commitment to their arduous
duty. The Committee duly acknowledges their patriotism. In this context, the Committee
strongly recommends that the Government should provide better conditions of living and
better conditions of service to BSF personnel. The Committee also recommends to the
Government to grant desert/remote areas allowance and ration money. The Government
should also expedite the opening of Kendriya Vidyalaya in the border areas so that the
education of the children of the BSF Jawans is not neglected on account of posting in
frontier areas.
2.3.2 The Committee also came across incidents of death of BSF personnel due to snake
bite coupled with the time taken to move the victims to hospital located far off from the
border. One of the solution that was suggested to the sub-Committee was that the BSF
personnel be provided with knee-high boots. The Committee, agreeing to the suggestion,
strongly, recommends that the Government should make a provision for supplying knee-
high boots to the BSF personnel.
2.3.3 The Committee is of the view that that the Ministry of Home Affairs should take
into account the geographical and topographical location of Jaisalmer and Barmer sectors
for chalking out logistic strategy for border surveillance and management. This sector is
one of the largest having an area of 470 kms. where BSF has been entrusted with the task
of taking care of 122 BOPs and 187 gates. Since the terrain of these sectors is sandy,
marred with permanent and shifting sand dunes of varying height of 10 to 50 metres, a well
chalked out strategy is the need of the hour. Regular maintenance and repairing of roads
would ensure continued surveillance of the border areas. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that Ministry of Home Affairs should provide a tractor to each company for
regular repairing and maintenance of roads along the border areas. The BSF should get the
required basic infrastructure for monitoring the border, for example, lateral and axial roads
upto the BOPs to enhance the operational efficiency. The task of surveillance should be
carefully examined so that effective monitoring mechanism is put in place. At present, one
Battalion is entrusted on an average with the task of manning 60-62 kms. which inhibits
operational efficiency. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Home
Affairs should look into the matter at the earliest.
2.3.4 The Committee was given to understand that about Rs. 3 crore was spent on water
supply for the BSF personnel. It was suggested that a water pipeline along the BOP line may
be provided for use of BSF personnel as well as for the wildlife and tree plantations. The

6
Committee agrees that laying of pipelines along the border would be economical as
compared to the supply of water by the water tankers and accordingly recommends the
same for early implementation.
2.3.5 The Committee notes that the place of worship in the border areas are closely
intertwined with daily life of BSF Jawans. It is of the considered view of the Committee that
if water tank/reservoirs/lakes could be constructed near such places of worship, it would to
a great extend solve the daily necessity of the Jawans as well as the cattle of the farmers.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs should come out
with suitable scheme for providing water tanks/reservoirs/lakes near the places of worship
located near the frontier areas.
2.4 The Sub-Committee visited Bhuj Sector on 1st July, 2007. The following issues came up
for special mention in the sector:
• The Gujarat sector of Bhuj has been entrusted to SHQ Bhuj to look after the border
along the Great Rann of Kutch and Creek areas. The international border between
Kutch on Indian side and Sind Province on the Pakistan side, has a total length of 301
kms. This border can be divided into three prominent segments (i) Land border in
Great Rann of Kutch (197 kms.); (ii) Creek Areas (36 kms.); (iii) Sir Creek (68 kms.).
• The terrain is salty waste land with no vegetation in the entire area-except on bets
(raised ground) where small bushes are available. The area gets inunadated with the
onset of monsoon as well as the underground configuration of land which restricts
absorption of water contents in it. Most of the area remains cut off from normal
activities due to inundation and difficulties of movement due to marshy and boggy
land.
• Scorching heat waves mixed with saline effect makes living conditions extremely
inhospitable.
• Creek areas are extremely difficult operational proposition where operations are
completely dependent upon the natural factors of tide timing which are related to lunar
activities. The area is totally marshy and swampy.
• The area of Sir Creek is disputed due to different perceptions of India and Pakistan.
It is navigable only during high tide by medium/mechanized crafts and Fast Patrol
Boats (FPBs). The IB runs along the mid-stream of Sir Creek. On the Pakistan side,
mainland is comparatively closer to Sir Creek, hence its vigil is much easier for Pak
forces.
• Pakistan has started showing added interest in this area and has got a good built up
of its forces opposite creek area. Due to dispute in the Sir Creek sector, a rogue
action by Pak cannot be ruled out. However, any major intrusion will be extremely
difficult due to marshy land and presence of mangroves.
• The most likely threat is of infiltration and smuggling through creeks. As the creeks
are inter-connected, once the enemy makes an entry to one of the major creeks from
the IB, he can move into any of the creeks in small craft.
• Under domination plan, patrolling by two FPBs supported by medium/mechanized
crafts deployed at Mal Creek/Nar Creek is done. Air Recce is carried out every
fortnight over the creek area. Unmanned Aerial vehicle (UAV) missions are also planned
and executed. Three Floating BOPs are also deployed at a time during fair weather at
certain locations.

7
• Emergency evacuation is done by IAF on requisition from BSF. No helicopters are
stationed at Bhuj/Naliya. Helicopter has to come from Jamnagar which will be reaching
at the place of incident after approx 2 1 to 3 hours after refuelling.
• A total of 28 BOPs were sanctioned, out of which 16 and 12 were required to be
constructed by CPWD and NBCC, respectively. Construction work of 3 BOPs had
been completed by the CPWD and remaining BOPs are under construction. However,
in regard to construction of 12 BOPs by NBCC, 11 are under construction and one
BOP is yet to be started.
• Regarding construction of border road, a total length of 134 kms. is required to be
constructed. Construction of 73.5 kms. and 60.5 kms. road has been allotted to
CPWD and NBCC, respectively. Out of 73.5 kms., CPWD had constructed 49 Kms.
of road. However, NBCC has not completed any work and construction of road by it
was underway.
• Link roads are also in bad shape. 90 kms. of link roads was required to be completed.
From Dharamshala to BOP Vigokot, 60 kms. of road was completed. However, it was
badly damaged due to heavy vehicular traffic of NBCC/CPWD and some portion of it
was repaired by CPWD. From Dharamshala to BOP Bediabet, construction of 19 kms.
has been completed. However, road was damaged due to the above mentioned reasons
and required immediate repair. Construction of remaining link roads is under progress
and there was need to expedite the work.
• Fencing work of 134 kms. had been sanctioned, out of which work on 73.5 Kms. and
60.5 kms. was to be done by the CPWD and NBCC, respectively. CPWD and NBCC
had completed fencing work on 37 kms. and 23 kms., respectively and work was in
progress on 68.55 kms. Work on the remaining 5.54 kms. has not started. The same
length of 134 kms. has been sanctioned for floodlighting work to be executed by
CPWD. Work on 47 Kms. was completed but the same was not functional. Work on
76 kms. was in progress and while work on 11 kms. was to be started.
2.4.1 The Sub-Committee in its meeting held on 22nd October, 2007 reviewed the progress made
in regard to border fencing works on Indo Pak border in Gujarat Sector.
2.4.2 As stated elsewhere in this report, the sub-Committee was informed that the Gujarat Sector
of Indo-Pak Border has got geo-climatic disadvantages for border fencing and floodlighting
projects. This sector faced disastrous earthquake in Bhuj area in 2001 followed by flood in 2003.
The area received unprecedented downpour in 2006-07 which led to the cost and time overrun of
the project. Besides, the devastating earthquake in 2001 had led to dislocation of entire logistics and
infrastructure and the 50 years’ record breaking flood has led to site inundation for more than a
year. The marshy land has got high degree of salinity which derailed the project of border fencing.
Moreover, ban on mining of stones and sand by the State Government delayed the projects in the
Tharad Sector as the material was to be carted from Rajasthan. All these conditions have led to
time and cost overrun of the projects. The sub-Committee was informed that due to non-release
of funds in time, the construction work had come to a standstill. Only a meager budget allocation
i.e., to the tune of Rs. 14 crore against total current demand of Rs. 101 crore upto the second
quarter of the last financial year, had been released.
2.4.3 As already stated in this report, the Sub-Committee was also informed that the final
anticipated revised cost stood to the tune of Rs. 1210 crore. The increase in the project was also
due to increase in the scope of work and escalation in the cost of construction material. Sanction
of the upgradation works and approval of the revised estimates were awaited since August 2007.
The project requires CCS approval for the revised cost of Rs. 1210 crore for border works in the
Gujarat Sector.

8
Observations/Recommendations
2.5.1 The Committee understands that the geographical and topographical location of the
region as well as remoteness and tough terrain conditions of Rann have greatly hampered
the border fencing and floodlighting projects. The final anticipated revised cost to the tune
of Rs. 1210 crore was under the consideration of CCS. The Committee recommends that the
revised cost may be expeditiously approved by CCS for early completion of the works.
2.5.2 The Committee observes that the existing system of emergency evacuation in the
Bhuj/Naliya sector by IAF on requisition from BSF is not a proper arrangement as the
helicopter has to fly to the place of incident from Jamnagar after refuelling. The term
‘emergency’ evacuation’ has no meaning as disaster will not wait for hours before it strikes.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that an alternative arrangement may be put in
place.
2.5.3 The Committee is constrained to observe that the work of construction of border
roads has not been taken up seriously. Out of total length of 134 kms. which was required
to be constructed, 73.5 Kms. road has been allotted to CPWD and 60.5 kms. to the NBCC.
Out of 73.5 kms, CPWD has constructed only 49 Kms. road. NBCC too has not completed
its work. The Committee strongly recommends that Government must make an inquiry into
the matter and direct the agencies concerned to complete the construction of border roads
without further delay, for effective patrolling of the border areas by BSF personnel.
2.5.4 The Committee further recommends that the construction of the remaining link
roads (to the extent of 21 kms.) be expedited. The reported wearing and tearing of the link
roads from Dharamshala to BOP Vigokot and Dharamshala to BOP Bediabet, due to heavy
vehicular traffic of NBCC/CPWD  need immediate attention for repair.
2.5.5 The Committee has been given to understand that Creek Sector is a porous border.
A number of small infiltration in collusion with anti-national elements and terrorists, enter
the country through this border. Smuggling of fake currency notes, narcotics, arms and
ammunition, explosives and trafficking of illegal immigrants, are some of the common anti-
national activities that are carried out through this area. Creek area is reportedly used as
a launch pad for terrorist activities and gathering information on patrolling pattern of the
country. All these activities indicate the nefarious design of the forces inimical to the
country’s interests, to widen the scope of terrorism to coastal areas. The Committee,
therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry of Home affairs should immediately pay
attention towards strengthening of the monitoring mechanism in the Bhuj Sector, and plug
the porous points in the border. Sooner it is done better it would be in the national interest.

CHAPTER-III
ON THE SPOT STUDY OF BORDER AREAS OF JAMMU AND PUNJAB
3.1 The Sub-Committee visited border areas of Jammu and Punjab from 25th to 28th May, 2008.
During its visit to Jammu, the following issues came up for special mention:—
• The Government decided to fence the Jammu International Border in 1994 and
sanctioned the project in March, 1995. The construction work was started by the
CPWD in July, 1995.
• Pakistan opposed erecting the fence as it considered the entire territory of J&K as
disputed and started heavy firing and shelling. Due to inability of CPWD to further
carry on with the project, the work was stopped just after 5 days.
• The project was finally entrusted to BSF in July, 2000, which started the work in
January, 2001. Pakistan again tried to stop the work by resorting to heavy firing and
shelling.
• To provide cover to the persons engaged in fencing work, the BSF first raised a
protective bund all along the border. Despite fierce opposition from Pakistan, the BSF
continued with the task and completed the project in November, 2005. 6 BSF personnel
were killed and 32 injured due to the Pakistani firing.
• The sanctioned cost of the project including floodlighting was Rs. 75.24 crore for a
length of 186 Kms. whereas the BSF managed to construct the same in Rs. 64.69
crore only.
• The fencing was done on emergent basis to check infiltration of militants. Due to firing
and shelling at some places, the fence had to be erected about 0.5 to 1.5 Kms. inside
Indian territory from the border. Therefore, a sizable chunk of agricultural land
remained ahead of the fence.
• After declaration of ceasefire in November, 2003, it was decided to realign 38 Kms.
of fence and shift it closure to the border to obviate the problems of farmers and bring
about 4300 acres of land inside the fencing. The work on the same was underway and
likely to be completed soon.
• Some farmers have represented that they have not been paid compensation for a long
time.
Observation/Recommendation
3.2.1 The Committee was apprised that the bund which was constructed in order to provide
security cover to the persons engaged in fencing work, had now become counterproductive
and was helping militants. It has been reported that Pakistan has made a lot of construction
after ceasefire. It had constructed 97 OP Towers and 162 barracks. The Committee,
therefore, strongly feels that Government of India should upgrade India’s border
surveillance and military preparedness.

10
3.3 The Sub-Committee visited border areas of Punjab on 26th and 27th May, 2008. It visited
Amritsar Sector on 26th and Ferozpur Sector on 27th May, 2008. The main issues that came up
for special mention are:—
• During the year 1989-93, 475 Kms. long fence and 468 Kms. long floodlighting along
the international border in Punjab Frontier was completed and handed over to BSF. The
border is maintained by battalions of BSF.
• Border belt of Punjab has two prominent rivers namely, Ravi and Sutlej which flows
to Pakistan alongwith several nallahs and its tributaries. The rivers, nallahs and
tributaries have created some gaps during the floods in past.
• Fence in these stretches has been washed away and there are 27 such gaps. There
are 373 gates out of which 240 gates were being opened and remaining 125 gates
were closed as there was Government land ahead of the fencing.
• Opening timings of the gates are 7.00 A.M. to 5.30 P.M. in summer and 8.00 A.M.
to 4.30 P.M. in winter. Average number of farmers crossing the gates per day is 1550.
Opening times are increased during sowing and harvesting seasons.
• Out of 475 Kms. of fencing in Punjab, 171 Kms. fencing has been done with concrete
base.
• In the Abohar and Ferozpur Sectors, the project of shifting about 22.5 Kms. of
fencing close to border with concrete base has been sanctioned and land acquisition
is under process. 32.3 Kms. long fencing is, also proposed to be shifted in Gurudaspur
Sector and the proposal is under consideration.
• There is need for upgradation of border floodlights. Most of the equipments have
outlived their life and cables have also been damaged due to various reasons. It has
been recommended to completely replace the existing Border Flood Light (BFL)
system. It has also been decided to execute a sample job on some stretch. The matter
is in progress.
• Recruitment of 685 women constables is under process and expected to be completed
shortly. These women constables are proposed to be deployed at the fencing gates for
frisking of women farmers.
Observation/Recommendation
3.4.1 Keeping in view the fact that the floodlight equipments have outlived their life and
cables have also become obsolete and damaged, the Committee recommends that it is
necessary to replace the existing Border Flood Light (BFL) system with utmost expedition.
3.5 The sub-Committee sought to know from the Ministry of Home Affairs the status of
realignment of Indo-Pak border fence towards the zero line.
3.5.1 The Ministry of Home Affairs in its communication dated 4th February, 2008 stated as
under:—
“Government of India has sanctioned the fencing of 186 kms. India-Pakistan Border
in Jammu sector. The construction of fencing on the India-Pakistan Border in Jammu was
executed by BSF within 150 yards from the International Border (IB) except in 38.015 kms.
stretch of International Border (IB), where fence was constructed at varied distances, from
400 mtrs. to 1.5 kms., due to heavy firing by Pakistan at the time of construction. However,

11
in view of the difficulties experienced by the farmers and for enhancing surveillance, the
proposal for forward shifting of this 38.015 kms. border fence, towards the IB, in Jammu
has since been approved by the Government and at present earth levelling work is in
progress. With the forward shifting of this stretch of fence, the problem faced by fanners
is expected to be minimized.”
Observations/Recommendations
3.6.1 The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs should take up the
issue of realigning the fence towards the zero line on top priority as large tracks of
cultivable lands lie beyond the present fencing area. The Committee also recommends that
shifting of fencing in Abohar and Ferozpur Sectors be completed in a scheduled time frame
and the proposal of shifting of fencing in Gurudaspur sector be finalized and approved at
the earliest.
3.6.2 It has been brought to the notice of the Committee that the Indian farmers sow the crops
in the large land located between the fencing line and international border areas which is very
fertile, unfortunately, during the harvest time the crops are taken away by the people from the
other side of the border with the connivance and support of the border guarding forces of the
neighboring country. The Committee is of the view that the problem being faced by our farmers
is expected to be minimized with the forward shifting of this stretch offence.
3.6.3 T he Committee further recommends that the recruitment of 685 women constables
to be deployed at the fencing gates for frisking of women farmers, should be completed at
the earliest so that no inconvenience is caused to the women farmers while being frisked.
3.6.4 The Committee has been officially informed that painting of fence is being done
regularly as per specifications and budget and for this purpose funds have been allocated
to the battalions. However, the sub-Committee has been given to understand that there are
some funds constraints in this regard. Considering the condition of weather in the area and
to avoid recurring cost, the Committee recommends that the composition of metal used in
the fence should be changed and fencing may be done by using good quality galvanized iron
or steel.
3.7 The farmers brought to the notice of the sub-Committee, the following problems being
faced by them, for redressal:—
• Farmers of BOP Chakri have requested for construction of pontoon bridge. One
pontoon bridge in the area of 109 Bn is required to be constructed over river Tarna.
• The border belt width has been increased from 5 to 16 Kms. from the IB. The Central
Government funds under BADP are spent in this enlarged border area, thus leaving
very little for actual border belt. The benefits of reservation have also been stretched
due to the above mentioned reasons at the cost of the actual residents of the border
belts.
• Bridge over Ravi river is urgently required at Kakkar village for farmers so that they
can cultivate their land trapped in Tota Enclave.
• Farmers are facing hardships in cultivating their land across the Sutlej river due to non
availability of bridges in some locations.
Observation/Recommendation
3.8.1 The Committee appreciates the hardship being faced by farmers in cultivating their

12
land beyond the rivers Tarna, Sutlej and Ravi. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
Government should explore the possibility of construction of a pontoon bridge at Chakri
over river Tarna, bridge over Ravi at Kakkar village and a bridge over Sutlej river.
3.9 The sub-Committee also visited Ferozpur Sector. The following issues came up for special
mention:—
• Like other sectors of Punjab region, cultivation is done upto zero line and there were
some undulating and broken ground at some places with bushy terrain and high growth
of Sarkanda.
• In this sector Sutlej and Kasur are the main water channels. However, there are no
washed away gaps. There are 114 gates and movement of farmers is regulated through
these gates.
• Total land ahead of fencing in the sector is about 15000 acre, out of which 12500 acre
private land and the remaining 2500 acre is Government land with about 150 Kms.
total length of signal fencing except double fencing of 6.6 Kms. at some BOPs. Only
64.5 Kms. fencing is with concrete base.
• There are some proposals for construction of Forward Command Posts which were
under consideration and there was compelling need for early decision.
• There is no Black Top (Pucca) road along the entire stretch of fencing of Punjab
Frontier which is restricting movement, hampering operations as well as adversely
affecting health of personnel.
• Pontoon bridges/belley bridges at some locations are required to facilitate movement of
BSF troops as well as farmers. Axial and lateral roads connecting border fence ‘“gates
at several places need to be constructed.
• One more battalion is required as the Ferozpur Sector is considered as hyper sensitive area.
Observation/Recommendation
3.10.1 The Committee expresses its serious concern over the absence of Black Top (pucca)
road along the entire stretch of fencing of Punjab Frontier. The sub-Committee would like
the Ministry of Home Affairs to look into this grey area and examine the possibility of
construction of pucca roads along the entire stretch of Punjab Frontier. The Committee
strongly. recommends that axial and lateral roads connecting border fence gates, are
required to be constructed for effective patrolling of the border areas.  The Committee is of
the strong view that pontoon bridges/belley bridges are also required to be constructed at
strategic locations to facilitate movement of BSF troops as well as farmers. The Committee
further recommends that the construction of pucca roads and their timely repairing would
improve better surveillance of border areas by the BSF and curbing of infiltration from other
side of the border area.
3.10.2 The Committee desires that the issue of raising one more battalion at the Ferozpur
Sector, may be examined in the Ministry of Home Affairs as this is a hyper sensitive area.
3.10.3 The Committee also urges upon the Ministry for an early decision on construction
of Forward Command post.
General Observations/recommendations
3.11.1 During the course of its study visit, the Committee had occasion to witness the

13
retreat ceremony at the  Wagha Border at Amritsar. The Committee observed that although
a large number of tourists flock this area for w itnessing the r etreat cer emony, the
infrastructure and amenities were inadequate. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
there is a need for upgrading amenities for the tourists. The Committee also had an
opportunity to visit JCP Hussainiwala. This place is also home to the Samadhis of Shaheed
Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev. However, this spot is less popular amongst the visitors.
Therefore, there is a need to popularize this place amongst the public. The Committee also
recommends that there is an urgent need for a longer gallery to accommodate more persons
to witness the retreat ceremony as the existing one can accommodate small number of
persons, at JCP Hussainiwala.
3.11.2 It is the understanding of the Sub-Committee that proper management of the Border
spells out many challenges viz.  co-ordination and concerted action by administrative,
diplomatic, security, intelligence, legal, regulatory and financial agencies of the country to
secure the frontiers and subserve its interests. Keeping in view these facts, the Committee
recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs should chalk out a strategic Action Plan
which may include construction of effective and quality fencing, floodlighting and concrete
roads along the border areas; deployment of high-tech surveillance equipments on the
border; strengthening of security of coastal borders of the country etc.

OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
STELLAR ROLE OF BSF IN GUARDING THE COUNTRY’S FRONTIERS
The Committee hails the stellar role of BSF in guarding the country’s frontiers under
tremendous adverse circumstances due to geographical, climatic and other conditions. Our
borders are secure due to their diligence, loyalty and commitment to their arduous duty. The
Committee duly acknowledges their patriotism. In this context, the Committee strongly
recommends that the Government should provide better conditions of living and better conditions
of service to BSF personnel. The Committee also recommends to the Government to grant
desert/remote areas allowance and ration money. The Government should also expedite the
opening of Kendriya Vidyalaya in the border areas so that the education of the children of the
BSF Jawans is not neglected on account of posting in frontier areas. (Para 2.3.1)
INCIDENTS OF DEATH OF BSF PERSONNEL DUE TO SNAKE BITE
The Committee also came across incidents of death of BSF personnel due to snake
bite coupled with the time taken to move the victims to hospital located far off from the
border. One of the solution that was suggested to the sub-Committee was that the BSF
personnel be provided with knee-high boots. The Committee, agreeing to the suggestion,
strongly, recommends that the Government should make a provision for supplying knee-
high boots to the BSF personnel. (Para 2.3.2)
LOGISTIC STRATEGY FOR BORDER SURVEILLANCE AND MANAGEMENT
The Committee is of the view that that the Ministry of Home Affairs should take
into account the geographical and topographical location of Jaisalmer and Barmer sectors
for chalking out logistic strategy for border surveillance and management. This sector is
one of the largest having an area of 470 kms. where BSF has been entrusted with the task
of taking care of 122 BOPs and 187 gates. Since the terrain of these sectors is sandy,
marred with permanent and shifting sand dunes of varying height of 10 to 50 metres, a well
chalked out strategy is the need of the hour. Regular maintenance and repairing of roads
would ensure continued surveillance of the border areas. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that Ministry of Home Affairs should provide a tractor to each company for
regular repairing and maintenance of roads along the border areas. The BSF should get the
required basic infrastructure for monitoring the border, for example, lateral and axial roads
upto the BOFs to enhance the operational efficiency. The task of surveillance should be
carefully examined so that effective monitoring mechanism is put in place. At present, one
Battalion is entrusted on an average with the task of manning 60-62 kms. which inhibits
operational efficiency. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Home
Affairs should look into the matter at the earliest. (Para 2.3.3)
WATER SUPPLY FOR THE BSF PERSONNEL
The Committee was given to understand that about Rs. 3 crore was spent on water
supply for the BSF personnel. It was suggested that a water pipeline along the BOP line may
be provided for use of BSF personnel as well as for the wildlife and tree plantations. The
Committee agrees that laying of pipelines along the border would be economical as
14

15
compared to the supply of water by the water tankers and accordingly recommends the
same for early implementation. (Para 2.3.4)
The Committee notes that the place of worship in the border areas are closely
intertwined with daily life of BSF Jawans. It is of the considered view of the Committee that
if water tank/reservoirs/lakes could be constructed near such places of worship, it would to
a great extend solve the daily necessity of the Jawans as well as the cattle of the farmers.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs should come out
with suitable scheme for providing water tanks/reservoirs/lakes near the places of worship
located near the frontier areas. (Para 2.3.5)
EXPEDITIOUS APPROVAL OF REVISED COST
The Committee understands that the geographical and topographical location of the
region as well as remoteness and tough terrain conditions of Rann have greatly hampered
the border fencing and floodlighting projects. The final anticipated revised cost to the
tune of Rs. 1210 crore was under the consideration of CCS. The Committee recommends
that the revised cost may be expeditiously approved by CCS for early completion of the
works. (Para 2.5.1)
EMERGENCY EVACUATION IN THE BHUJ/NALIYA SECTOR
The Committee observes that the existing system of emergency evacuation in the
Bhuj/Naliya sector by IAF on requisition from BSF is not a proper arrangement as the
helicopter has to fly to the place of incident from Jamnagar after refuelling. The term
‘emergency evacuation’ has no meaning as disaster will not wait for hours before it strikes.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that an alternative arrangement may be put in
place. (Para 2.5.2)
COMPLETION OF THE CONSTRUCTION OF BORDER ROADS WITHOUT FURTHER DELAY
The Committee is constrained to observe that the work of construction of border
roads has not been taken up seriously. Out of total length of 134 Kms. which was required
to be constructed, 73.5 Kms. road has been allotted to CPWD and 60.5 Kms. to the NBCC.
Out of 73.5 Kms., CPWD has constructed only 49 Kms. road. NBCC too has not completed
its work. The Committee strongly recommends that Government must make an inquiry
into the matter and direct the agencies concerned to complete the construction of border
roads without further delay, for effective patrolling of the border areas by BSF personnel.
(Para 2.5.3)
EXPEDITIOUS CONSTRUCTION OF THE REMAINING LINK ROADS
The Committee further recommends that the construction of the remaining link
roads (to the extent of 21 kms.) be expedited. The reported wearing and tearing of the link
roads from Dharamshala to BOP Vigokot and Dharamshala to BOP Bediabet, due to heavy
vehicular traffic of NBCC/CPWD  need immediate attention for repair. (Para 2.5.4)
STRENGTHENING OF THE MONITORING MECHANISM IN THE BHUJ SECTOR
The Committee has been given to understand that Creek Sector is a porous border.
A number of small infiltration in collusion with anti-national elements and terrorists, enter
the country through this border. Smuggling of fake currency notes, narcotics, arms and
ammunition, explosives and trafficking of illegal immigrants, are some of the common anti-

16
national activities that are carried out through this area. Creek area is reportedly used as
a launch pad for terrorist activities and gathering information on patrolling pattern of the
country. All these activities indicate the nefarious design of the forces inimical to the
country’s interests, to widen the scope of terrorism to coastal areas. The Committee,
therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry of Home affairs should immediately pay
attention towards strengthening of the monitoring mechanism in the Bhuj Sector, and plug
the porous points in the border. Sooner it is done better it would be in the national interest.
(Para 2.5.5)
UPGRADING INDIA’S BORDER SURVEILLANCE AND MILITARY PREPAREDNESS
The Committee was apprised that the bund which was constructed in order to provide
security cover to the persons engaged in fencing work, had now become counterproductive
and was helping militants. It has been reported that Pakistan has made a lot of construction
after ceasefire. It had constructed 97 OP Towers and 162 barracks. The Committee,
therefore, strongly feels that Government of India should upgrade India’s border
surveillance and military preparedness. (Para 3.2.1)
REPLACEMENT OF THE EXISTING BORDER FLOOD LIGHT (BFL) SYSTEM
Keeping in view the fact that the floodlight equipments have outlived their life and
cables have also become obsolete and damaged, the Committee recommends that it is
necessary to replace the existing Border Flood Light (BFL) system with utmost expedition.
(Para 3.4.1)
REALIGNING THE FENCE TOWARDS THE ZERO LINE ON TOP PRIORITY
The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs should take up the
issue of realigning the fence towards the zero line on top priority as large tracks of
cultivable lands lie beyond the present fencing area. The Committee also recommends that
shifting of fencing in Abohar and Ferozpur Sectors be completed in a scheduled time-frame
and the proposal of shifting of fencing in Gurudaspur sector be finalized and approved at
the earliest. (Para 3.6.1)
It has been brought to the notice of the Committee that the Indian farmers sow the
crops in the large land located between the fencing line and international border areas
which is very fertile, unfortunately, during the harvest time the crops are taken away by
the people from the other side of the border with the connivance and support of the border
guarding forces of the neighbouring country. The Committee is of the view that the problem
being faced by our farmers is expected to be minimized with the forward shifting of this
stretch of fence. (Para 3.6.2)
WOMEN CONSTABLES TO BE DEPLOYED AT THE FENCING GATES FOR FRISKING OF
WOMEN FARMERS
The Committee further recommends that the recruitment of 685 women constables
to be deployed at the fencing gates for frisking of women farmers should be completed at
the earliest so that no inconvenience is caused to the women farmers while being frisked.
(Para 3.6.3)
CHANGE IN COMPOSITION OF METAL USED IN THE FENCE
The Committee has been officially informed that painting of fence is being done
regularly as per specifications and budget and for this purpose funds have been allocated

17
to the battalions. However, the Committee has been given to understand that there are
some funds constraints in this regard. Considering the condition of weather in the area and
to avoid recurring cost, the Committee recommends that the composition of metal used in
the fence should be changed and fencing may be done by using good quality galvanized iron
or steel. (Para 3.6.4)
CONSTRUCTION OF A PONTOON BRIDGE
The Committee appreciates the hardship being faced by farmers in cultivating their
land beyond the rivers Tarna, Sutlej and Ravi. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
Government should explore the possibility of construction of a pontoon bridge at Chakri
over river Tarna, bridge over Ravi at Kakkar village and a bridge over Sutlej river.
(Para 3.8.1)
CONSTRUCTION OF PUCCA ROADS ALONG THE ENTIRE STRETCH OF PUNJAB FRONTIER
The Committee expresses its serious concern over the absence of Black Top (Pucca)
road along the entire stretch of fencing of Punjab Frontier. The Committee would like the
Ministry of Home Affairs to look into this grey area. and examine the possibility of
construction of pucca roads along the entire stretch of Punjab Frontier. The Committee
strongly recommends that axial and lateral roads connecting border fence gates, are
required to be constructed for effective patrolling of the border areas.  The Committee is of
the strong view  that pontoon bridges/belley bridges are also required to be constructed at
strategic locations to facilitate movement of BSF troops as well as farmers. The Committee
further recommends that the construction of pucca roads and their timely repairing would
improve better surveillance of border areas by the BSF and curbing of infiltration from
other side of the border area. (Para 3.10.1)
ONE MORE BATTALION AT THE FEROZPUR SECTOR
The Committee desires that the issue of raising one more battalion at the Ferozpur
Sector, may be examined in the Ministry of Home Affairs as this is a hyper sensitive area.
(Para 3.10.2)
CONSTRUCTION OF FORWARD COMMAND POST
The Committee also urges upon the Ministry for an early decision on construction
of Forward Command post. (Para 3.10.3)
UPGRADING AMENITIES FOR THE TOURISTS
During the course of its study visit, the sub-Committee had occasion to witness the
retreat ceremony at the Wagha Border at Amritsar. The Committee observed that although
a large number of tourists flock this area for w itnessing the r etreat cer emony, the
infrastructure and amenities were inadequate. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
there is a need for upgrading amenities for the tourists. The Committee also had an
opportunity to visit JCP Hussainiwala. This place is also home to the Samadhis of Shaheed
Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev. However, this spot is less popular amongst the visitors.
Therefore, there is a need to popularize this place amongst the public. The Committee also
recommends that there is an urgent need for a longer gallery to accommodate more persons
to witness the retreat ceremony as the existing one can accommodate small number of
persons, at JCP Hussainiwala. (Para 3.11.1)

18
CHALLENGES IN PROPER MANAGEMENT OF THE BORDER
It is the understanding of the Committee that proper management of the Border
spells out many challenges viz.  co-ordination and concerted action by administrative,
diplomatic, security, intelligence, legal, regulatory and financial agencies of the country to
secure the frontiers and subserve its interests. Keeping in view these facts, the Committee
recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs should chalk out a strategic Action Plan
which may include construction of effective and quality fencing, floodlighting and concrete
roads along the border areas; deployment of high-tech surveillance equipments on the
border; strengthening of security of coastal borders of the country etc. (Para 3.11.2)

Nepal border as there were reports of large scale smuggling of arms and drugs due to its porosity.
He also examined about per Km cost of expenditure on fencing and about smuggling of coal from
India through Meghalaya border. Secretary, Border Management replied that at present there was
no proposal to fence Indo Nepal border. He however said that the border had been strengthened
by posting SSB there. Earlier State Police were performing that function. The Secretary apprised
the Committee that about Rupees 70 lakhs was the cost of fencing per kilometre.
7. One Member enquired why bridges, floodlights were not provided on border roads and why
fencing was done 150 yards away from IB/Zero point. He also enquired about rehabilitation of
those persons whose land had been acquired for fencing and if border fencing was considered a
defence structure. Secretary, BM responded that bridges and floodlighting were there on roads and
not on fencing areas. He also responded by saying that fencing at 150 yards was based on some
understanding between India and Bangladesh and that it was no a defence structure.

structure instead of fencing as fencing required huge recurring expenditure and had limited lifespan.

recurring expenses as coating etc. were done by consulting experts in the field.

PREFACE
I, the Chairperson of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home
Affairs, having been authorized by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred and Thirty-sixth Report on Revamping and Revitalization of Civil Defence
in the Country pertaining to the Ministry of Home Affairs.
2. The Sub-Committee on Civil Defence and Rehabilitation of J&K Migrants of Department-
related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs was constituted on 13th April, 2007 for
in-depth examination of the Civil Defence System in the country and the rehabilitation measures
taken by the Government for the J&K Migrants. The Sub-Committee was reconstituted on
9th August, 2007.
3. The Sub-Committee in its meeting held on 16th October, 2007 heard the official presentation
of the Secretary, Border Management, Ministry of Home Affairs on the subject. In that
presentation, the Sub-Committee was briefed of the background, aims and objectives, organizational
structure including the current status of Civil Defence set up in the country, categorization of Civil
Defence Towns, inherent weaknesses in the present set-up, new role in changed scenario and about
the changed policy perception towards Civil Defence. The Sub-Committee was also informed that
the Ministry of Home Affairs had constituted a one man High Power Committee headed by
Shri K.M. Singh, a former Director General of CISF and a Member of National Disaster
Management Authority, who had submitted a report titled ‘Revamping of Civil Defence in the
Country: National. Policy Approach Paper’ in December, 2006 containing a series of
recommendations for revitalization and revamping of Civil Defence in the country.
4. The Sub-Committee has presented its Report to the Committee based on the official
presentation on 16th October, 2007, the clarifications given by the representatives of MHA during
the said meeting to the queries raised by its members, the recommendations made in the High
Power Committee Report and the ATR thereon supplied by the Ministry of Home Affairs.
5. The Committee in its meeting held on 15th October, 2008 considered and adopted the
report.

REPORT
1.0 HISTORICAL BACKGROUND
1.1 According to the Background Note submitted by the Ministry of Home Affairs, Civil
Defence in our country owes its origin to erstwhile Air Raid Precaution (RAP) Organisation raised
and operated during World War II by the Ministry of Defence, to safeguard the life and property
of the civilian population and also to maintain the continuity of productive and economic activity
of the nation during the war time. It was wound up after World War II in 1945. In 1956,
Government of India, in consultation with the State Governments, planned establishment of an
“Emergency Relief Board” for rendering aid to people affected by natural calamities like floods,
famine and epidemic etc. The Board comprised of official and non-official members with Minister
of Home Affairs as its Chairman. Based on the decision taken by the Board, “Emergency Relief
Organisation” was established in 1956 to meet such emergencies/eventualities.
1.2 The policy of the Government of India, till the Chinese aggression and declaration of
Emergency in 1962, was confined to making the States and Union T erritories conscious of the need
of Civil Defence measures and to ask them to keep ready Civil Defence paper plans for major cities
and towns. Two major events which gave fillip to formalization of Civil Defence in India since
independence, were the Chinese aggression in November, 1962 and the Indo-Pak conflict in 1965
during which the nation was subjected to enemy air attacks. The Civil Defence, which earlier
operated under the now defunct “Defence of India Act 1962” was given legal status by” Civil
Defence Act” passed in 1968.
2.0 CHANGING NOTION OF CIVIL DEFENCE
2.1 During the course of presentation, the Ministry of Home Affairs apprised the Sub-
Committee that the definition of Civil Defence includes:—
“any measures, not amounting to actual combat, for affording protection to any person,
property, place or thing against any hostile attack.
‘Hostile Attack’ means any attack by any person or body of persons, during war, external
aggression, internal disturbances or otherwise which endangers the security of any life,
property, place or thing.”
2.2 The Sub-Committee was further apprised of the aims of the Civil Defence which are as
under:—
(i) to save life;
(ii) to minimize damage to property;
(iii) to maintain continuity of production; and
(iv) to keep up the high morale of public.
2.3 The present role of Civil Defence, in terms of the Civil Defence Act, 1968 is to provide
protection to individuals, properties and establishments against any “hostile attack”. The sub-
Committee was also informed that the MHA vide order dated 5 September, 2003, conveyed its
approval to the State Governments to utilize the services of Civil Defence volunteers for mitigation,
prevention and preparedness for disaster and also for response and relief after a disaster struck.
In pursuance of this order, Civil Defence is utilized by some of the States not only in response

2
activities during disaster, but also in pre-disaster activities, particularly in the field of community
capacity building and generating public awareness.
3.0 ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE
3.1 The Ministry of Home Affairs informed the Sub-Committee that the organizational structure
of Civil Defence is as under:—
(i) At the national level, the Director General Civil Defence under the Ministry of Home
Affairs is responsible for formulating Civil Defence policies and for coordination
thereof;
(ii) In the States, the Civil Defence is set up headed by a senior police officer designated
as the Director Civil Defence; and
(iii) At the district level, the District Magistrate/Deputy Commissioner of Police (DCP) of
a district is designated as Controller of Civil Defence.
4.0 CURRENT STATUS OF CIVIL DEFENCE SET UP
4.1 The Ministry stated that the following is the current status of Civil Defence in the
country:—
(i) Out of the 225 categorised CD towns, only 121 have so far been activated. (The
list is enclosed at Annexure-A). As a result, as against the target of 12.98 lakh
volunteers, only about 6.64 lakh have been enrolled so far and 4.84 lakh trained;
(ii) Only 17 States are having Central Training Institutes (CTIs) and most of them are
combined training institutes for Civil Defence and Home Guards;
(iii) M any of these training institutions are virtually non-functional because of lack of
funds and infrastructure. In addition, due to non-availability of funds, a sizeable
number of posts of permanent staff in CD set-ups remain vacant;
(iv) Many of the units do not have adequate transport, proper communication network
and other infrastructure including a proper control room for their day-to-day
functioning;
(v) No Civil Defence set up exists in Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland,
Kerala, Tamil Nadu and UT of Dadar and Nagar Haveli, Daman and Diu,
Lakshadweep and Puducherry; and
(vi) Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Gujarat, Jammu and Kashmir, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh,
Maharashtra, Orissa, Jharkhand and UT of Andaman and Nicobar have deficiency of
50% volunteers.

6.0 FUNDING MECHANISM OF CIVIL DEFENCE
6.1 During the course of the discussions, the Sub-Committee was told of the funding
mechanism for regulating civil defence in the country which is as under:—
Although, as part of the overall Defence preparedness, Civil Defence is in the Union List,
the responsibility for raising and training the Civil Defence set up has been given to the States. The
Central Government reimburses 25% of the cost of raising, training and equipping Civil Defence
corps.
6.2 To help the State Government, the Central Government reimburses, in the form of grants-
in-aid, some part of the expenditure incurred on the authorized items for raising and training of
volunteers, other equipment and services. Till 1991-92, Government of India was incurring 100%
expenditure in respect of all NE States including Assam and Sikkim and 5 Northern districts of
West Bengal. For other States, the sharing pattern was 50:50. It was revised every year upto
1996-97, from which year, the reimbursement is at the rate of 50% for six North East States
except Assam and Arunachal Pradesh. It is at the rate of 25% for all the other States. A sum of
Rs.12 crore each year during 2005-06 and 2006-07 was reimbursed to the States for this purpose
as against an annual amount of Rs.10 crores during the preceding year 2004-05.
6.3 The Sub-Committee was informed that during the year 2006-07 and 2007-08, budget
allocated for the purpose of Civil Defence was to the tune of Rs.12.00 crore for each financial
year. It was further informed that the Central Government reimburses expenditure on raising,
equipping and training of volunteers.
7.0 RECOMMENDATIONS OF GROUP OF MINISTERS
7.1 In this context it would be appropriate to consider the recommendations made by the Group
of Ministers constituted to look into issues of reforming the National Security System which had
also emphasized the need of revamping and strengthening the Civil Defence system. The
recommendation of Group of  Ministers is as follows:—
“During times of war, natural calamities and other similar emer gencies, Civil Defence
Organization has traditionally played a vital role in guarding the hinterland, supporting the
Armed Forces, mobilizing the citizens and in helping civil administration discharge its
responsibilities. Over the years, however, new and complex changes have emerged; the
preparedness of Civil Defence Personnel has also suffered. Therefore, it is, for the Ministry
of Home Affairs to carry out in-depth review of the organization’s effectiveness, identify
its weakness and the new challenges it will be required to meet, in the contemporary
scenario and evolve a concrete action plan to revamp it. This important task needs to be
undertaken in close collaboration with the State Governments. It is advisable to complete
this exercise on an urgent basis”.

8.0 J.C. PANT COMMITTEE
8.1 In the year 2001, a High Power Committee (HPC) under the Chairmanship of Shri J.C. Pant
was constituted which also recommended involvement of Civil Defence in Disaster Management.
The relevant recommendations of the Pant Committee are as below:
“The Central Government, under section 3 (1) (z), may ‘make rules regarding
utilization of Civil Defence Corps in disaster response so that they remain in a state of
continuous preparedness. A comprehensive role for all these services should be formalized
in a harmonized structure for Disaster Management. All the services should be integrated
into the State Disaster Management Plan and work under the concerned State Department
for Disaster Management. The State Disaster Management Act, being enacted, should
include the Civil Defence as one of the agencies of relief and rehabilitation.
State Governments may be permitted to accept donations for Civil Defence from
corporate sectors. The Chief Wardens of Civil Defence in every town should be accorded
appropriate status in Civil Administration hierarchy, especially with regard to their role and
importance in Disaster Management. Their services when utilized should be properly
recognized. To have a multi disciplinary unit, which will come into motion for activating and
following up various functions and responsibilities entrusted to DG CD under the Union War
Book during war, and to manage disasters, separate budgetary provision to be made for
Disaster Management related training, equipping and storing for these services. CD, Home
Guards and Fire Services should be placed under the administrative and operational control
of the state level management agency.”
9.0 SECRETARY, BORDER MANAGEMENT (BM) COMMITTEE
9.1 In pursuance of the recommendations of the GOM, a Committee under the Chairmanship
of Secretary, BM was constituted in the MHA. This Committee suggested revamping of the Civil
Defence organization to provide contemporary Disaster Management skills and preparedness in the
country. The Salient features of the recommendations of this committee were:
(a) Construction of 32 training institutes.
(b) Procurement of transport and equipment for the training institutes.
(c) Construction of administrative blocks/buildings for categorized Civil Defence towns.
(d) Enhancement of central share and also enhancement of duty/training allowances.
(e) Creation of additional posts in the office of the Director General Civil Defence (DGCD), MHA.
10.0 HOME MINISTER’S DIRECTIONS
10.1 While examining the recommendations of the Secretary BM Committee Report it was felt
that an examination of the Civil Defence concept and role was needed in order to make the Civil
Defence an effective instrument of civil safety in which Disaster Management should play a
prominent role. With this objective in view, Union Home Minister chaired a meeting on Civil
Defence on 5 January, 2006 wherein he desired that the Civil Defence set-up should be
strengthened and its scope widened to include Disaster Management and also to integrate National
Cadet Corps (NCC) in Civil Defence activities. In this context, he directed that a National Policy
Approach Paper should be formulated on the subject by one of the Members of NDMA.
11.0 NATIONAL POLICY APPROACH PAPER
11.1 The representatives of the Ministry of Home Affairs during their presentation briefed the

5
Sub-Committee of some inherent deficiencies in the civil defence apparatus which inter-alia
included lack of popularization of the concept and awareness of the people towards civil defence,
lack of training, legal infirmities, financial crunch and problem pertaining to sharing of expenditure
between Central Government and the State Governments. The present status of the Civil Defence
in terms of image, relevance and efficacy is characterized by inactivity and low morale. According
to the Ministry, the National Policy Approach Paper on “Revamping of Civil Defence in the
Country” prepared by the High Power Committee headed by Shri K.M. Singh
α  a highlighted
following deficiencies in the Civil Defence services and activities:—
(i) Civil Defence is perceived as an activity only during war. Since there has been no
war affecting the lives of people in CD towns during the last three decades, the
organization has lost its relevance in the eyes of the community as also the State
administration.
(ii) Civil Defence suffers from low morale as volunteers who had enrolled themselves in
the past had primarily been motivated by patriotic considerations. The chance to get
some social prestige on account of their proximity to the district administration was
an added incentive. However, over a period of time, not only has the patriotic
sentiment receded to the background, the volunteers have also felt neglected by the
district administration.
(iii) Civil Defence lacks proper recognition. The volunteers come from various sections
of society and many of them have a good social standing. They have been rendering
useful services during various crises situations. However, there is no system of
adequate and institutionalized recognition to these people. This has adversely affected
the participation of the general public in Civil Defence activities.
(iv) Since the requirement of Civil Defence does not have regular activity, it has been
increasingly perceived as irrelevant. There has been a steady decline in the activities
of the organization, in terms of training, mock drills and exercises. This has, in turn,
led to a lack of interest on the part of even active volunteers”
(v) People in general are not aware of the role and functions of Civil Defence. There
is hardly any publicity or awareness programmes to enlighten the general public
about the various activities of Civil Defence. This results in their apathy in
volunteering their services to Civil Defence.
(vi) There is apparent apathy of State Governments towards Civil Defence engineering as
not only do a number of sanctioned posts in the Civil Defence set-up remain unfilled,
but many of the personnel posted are also those who are not found very useful for
the normal policing duties.
(vii) Civil Defence in the States suffers from lack of motivation in the regular staff. The
success of the Civil Defence organization is very much dependant upon selection of
suitable volunteers with aptitude and motivation for voluntary work. This calls for
painstaking efforts on the part of regular CD staff in terms of talent spotting and
motivating. Since most of the regular CD staff themselves lack requisite initiative and
motivation, the process of selection and enlistment of right type of volunteers has
been a casualty.

12.0 RECOMMENDATIONS OF K.M. SINGH COMMITTEE
12.1 The following were the important recommendations made by the K.M. Singh Committee in
the above mentioned Approach Paper:—
• Civil Defence infrastructure may be made available in all the districts in the country
in a phased manner in the next three financial years. While doing this, the entire
concept and orientation of Civil Defence coverage has to be changed from ‘Town
Specific to District Specific’ with the area of responsibility covering the entire
district. In extending the scope of Civil Defence coverage to all the districts, the recent
report of Building Materials Technology Promotion Council (BMTPC), classifying 241
districts in the country as multi-hazard districts, is suggested to be taken as the base
and these 241 districts are proposed to be included in the initial stages.
• Civil Defence set-up should take up the implementation of the proposed new role in
community capacity building and public awareness in close coordination with the
Panchayati Raj Institution (PRI) and urban local bodies. It is also recommended that
the proposed new role of Civil Defence related to community building may be
integrated with the ongoing UNDP-Disaster Risk Management (DRM) project of
MHA.
• National Cadet Corps (NCC), Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangthan (NYKS), and National
Service Scheme (NSS), are also proposed to be integrated in the overall Disaster
Management framework with linkages with the Civil Defence set-up at the state head
quarters and district head quarters.
• Revamp the existing structure of Civil Defence by enhancing its functional and
territorial responsibilities in a realistic and cost-effective manner.
• Authorization of approximately 800 wardens per district of average 20 lakh
population is recommended, which would amount to total number of 4,80,000
wardens in the country.
• Civil Defence set-ups at all levels should be permitted to accept donations from the
corporate sector, as any contribution by the corporate sector on Civil Defence
activities and Civil Defence training programmes may be exempted from payment of
taxes, as appropriate, by the Finance Ministry.

• Total non-recurring expenditure relating to infrastructure (expect land, to be provided
by States) equipment and transport (Rs.2.69 crores for each Civil Defence Training
Institute) and Rs.1.90 crores for each Civil Defence Training School (CDTS), total
Rs.72.42 crores may be borne by the centre.
• The trainees at CD training institutions are presently being paid a meager allowance
of Rs. 28/- per day. This was recommended to be enhanced to Rs. 150/- per day.
13.0 FOLLOW-UP ACTION ON K.M. SINGH COMMITTEE REPORT
13.1 The Ministry informed the Sub-Committee that since the report proposed financial burden
on the States as well as restructuring of the organization and creation of 17 posts per district in
the States, consultation with the States was necessary. Consultation with Ministry of Defence was
also required as Civil Defence is considered an integral part of defence of the country. The
consultation process began in the month of January, 2007 and a copy of the report had been sent
by NDMA to all the Chief Secretaries and Directors General of Police. The Ministry of Home
Affairs had also started the process of consultation at two levels. The Director General of Civil
Defence held consultation with the officials of the State Governments during February, 2007. MHA
had solicited the views/comments of the State Governments.
13.2 In regard to the status of implementation of  the recommendations contained in the K.M.
Singh Committee Report, the Ministry of Home Affairs furnished the following information:—
(i) The recommendations contained in report of the Committee constituted by Ministry
of Home Affairs under the Chairmanship of Shri K.M. Singh, Member, NDMA, were
examined by the ‘Home Minister’s Civil Defence Advisory Committee’ chaired by the
Union Home Minister in its meeting held on 2nd April, 2008. The Advisory
Committee decided as under:—
1. Civil Defence should play a vital role in disaster management in accordance with the
recommendations of K.M.  Singh Committee.
2. The Ministry of Home Affairs should implement the project for Revamping of Civil
Defence at an estimated cost of Rs . 100 crore.
3. Civil Defence Act, 1968 may be amended to cater to the needs of disaster
management and internal security/terrorism related challenges.
(ii) Based on the recommendations of the Committee, MHA has drawn up a project
proposal for ‘Revamping of Civil Defence’ to be implemented during the Eleventh
Plan period at a total estimated cost of Rs.100 crore. The overall objective of the
scheme is to strengthen and revitalize the Civil Defence set up in the country so as
to play a significant role in disaster management and assisting the police in internal
security and law and order situation while retaining their primary role.
The scheme envisages strengthening of existing training institutes in 20 States/
UTs. The Scheme also envisages strengthening/transformation of Civil Defence set
up in 100 hazard prone districts in 16 identified States where training institutes are
existing.
(iii) An allocation of Rs.5.0 crore has been made for this scheme in BE 2008-09. This
is presently under the process of scrutiny/appraisal. After the appraisal, the scheme
will be put up to the competent authority for obtaining approval. It is expected that
the implementation would be initiated in the third quarter of 2008-09.
(iv) Amendments to the Civil Defence Act, 1968, as recommended by the ‘Home
Minister’s Civil Defence Advisory Committee’ are also being processed.
