8.6 It would be appropriate to go back to the legislative history and intent of the Constitution
Seventh-third and Seventy-fourth Amendments which sought to restore the rightful place in political
governance for local bodies and to provide a constitutional status to such bodies.
8.7 The Government introduced the Constitution (Seventy-second Amendment) Bill, 1991 in the
Lok Sabha on 16.9.1991. The Bill sought to insert Part IX and Eleventh Schedule to the
Constitution for the constitution of panchayats at the village, intermediate and district levels. The
Bill was referred to the Joint Committee which presented its report on 14.7.1992. The Bill as
reported by the Joint Committee was debated in the Lok Sabha on 1
st, 2 nd, 4 th, 21 st and 22 nd
December, 1992 and on 23 rd December, 1992 in the Rajya Sabha. The Bill, after being passed by
7 L.S. Deb dated  20.12.1991, c. 1189
8 L.S. Deb dated 21.12.1991, c. 263

24
both the Houses was ratified by the State Legislatures as per the requirement of proviso to Article
368 (2). After receiving Presidential assent, the Bill was enacted as the Constitution (Seventy-third
Amendment) Act, 1992 and came into force on 24.4.1993.
8.8 The relevant extracts from the Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill are reproduced
below:
“Article 40 of the Constitution which enshrines one of the Directive Principles of State
Policy, lays down that the State shall take steps to organize village panchayats and vest
them with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as
units of self-government. In the light of the experience of the last forty years and in view
of the shortcomings which have been observed, it was considered that there was an
imperative need to enshrine in the Constitution certain basic and essential features of
Panchayati Raj Institutions to impart certainty, continuity and strength to them.
Accordingly, it was proposed to add a new Part relating to Panchayats in the
Constitution to provide for, among other things, Gram Sabha in village or group of villages,
constitution of Panchayats at village and other level or levels, direct elections to all seats
in Panchayats at the village and intermediate levels, if any.”
9
8.9 Subsequently, the Constitution (Seventy-third Amendment) Bill, 1991 was introduced in the
Lok Sabha on 16
th September, 1991. The Bill sought to insert part IXA and Twelfth Schedule in
the Constitution relating to the constitution and composition of urban local bodies. The Bill was
referred to the Joint Committee which presented its report on 14
th July, 1992. The Bill, as reported
by Joint Committee, was debated in both the Houses of Parliament, along with the Constitution
(Seventy-second Amendment) Bill, 1991. After being passed by both Houses of Parliament, the Bill
was ratified by the State Legislatures as per the requirement of proviso to Article 368(2). After
receiving the Presidential assent, the Bill was enacted as the Constitution (Seventy-fourth
Amendment) Act, 1992 and came into force on 1.6.1993.
8.10 The relevant extracts from the SOR of the Bill are reproduced below:–
“In many States, local bodies have become weak and ineffective on account of a variety
of reasons, including the failure to hold regular elections, prolonged suppression and
inadequate devolution of powers and functions. As a result, Urban and Local Bodies are not
able to perform effectively as vibrant democratic units of self-government.
Having regard to these inadequacies, it was considered necessary that provisions relating
to Urban Local Bodies be incorporated in the Constitution, particularly, for:
(i) putting on a firmer footing the relationship between the State Government and the
Urban Local Bodies with respect to:
(a) the functions and taxation powers; and
(b) arrangements for revenue sharing;
(ii) ensuring regular conduct of elections;
(iii) ensuring timely elections in the case of supersession; and
(iv) providing adequate representation for the weaker sections and Scheduled Castes,
Scheduled Tribes and women.
Accordingly, it was proposed to add a new Part relating to the Urban Local Bodies in the
Constitution to provide for……”

8.16.1 However, it is interesting to note that in its Sixth Report on “Local Governance: An
Inspiring Journey into the Future”, the Second Administrative Reforms Commission, considered and
emphasized the core principles of local governance i.e. application of the principle of subsidiarity
in the context of decentralization; clear delineation of functions of local governments vis-à-vis State
Governments and among different tiers of local governments; effective devolution of these
functions and resources accompanied by capacity-building and accountability; integrated view of
local services and development through convergence of programmes and agencies and above
all, ‘citizen-centricity’.
24 The Commission in this regard made the following observation/
recommendation:
“Article 243C(3)(c) and (d) stipulates that the State Legislature may by law provide for the
representation of the Members of Parliament and State Legislature of the State at levels
other than the village level. The Commission is of the view that the imposing presence of
Members of Parliament and the State Legislature in the Panchayats would subdue the
emergence of local leadership which is a sine qua non  for development of vibrant local
governments. Therefore, the Commission is of the view that Members of Parliament and
State Legislatures should not become members of local bodies. This would endow the local
bodies with decision-making capabilities.”

8.16.2  The Committee finds that the observations and recommendations of the Second
ARC, made in its 6 th and 15 th Reports, contradict each other.
8.17 Be that as it may, it is ironical that while the government has heavily relied on the
Balakrishnan Committee Report in justifying the stand taken by it that in view of the
special characteristics of the NDMC area, the Council cannot be made an elected body, it
has ignored the spirit of the recommendations of that Committee for restructuring the
composition of the Council with nominated as well as equal number of elected members on
the basis of adult franchise. It needs also to be observed that while citing the
recommendations of the Estimates Committee (14
th Lok Sabha) as one of the grounds for
bringing in the amendment Bill, the Government has bye-passed the essence of that
Committee’s recommendation for reviewing the desirability of modifying the compositions of
the Council as recommended by the Balakrishnan Committee keeping in view the basic
democratic principles. It needs further to be pointed out that the Government has
conveniently used the recommendations made by the Second ARC in its Fifteenth Report
in taking the stand that the present governance structure of NDMC should not be changed
while disregarding the observations made by the said Commission in discussing the core
principles of Local Governance and the recommendations made by it in the context of
discussion on common issues, as contained in its Sixth Report.
8.18 For seventy eight long years i.e., from 1916 till the enactment of the NDMC Act 1994,
NDMC was governed by the provisions of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911. In discussing the
history of the NDMC, the Balakrishnan Committee Report, has referred to Section 11 of the Punjab
Municipal Act, 1911. The relevant extracts from the Balakrishnan Committee Report are in this
context, reproduced below:
“ ….under Section 11 of that Act a Municipal Committee is to consist of not less than five
members either appointed by the State Government or elected from among the inhabitants
of partly of the one and partly of the other. However, the appointed members shall not
ordinarily be more than one fourth of the total members. One of its members is to be
elected as President of Committee, and one or two of its member as Vice-President or Vice-
Presidents……”
26
8.19 The Committee would like to point out that the law which formed the basis of the
composition and functioning of the NDMC for nearly eight decades, provided for a substantial
component of members elected from amongst the inhabitants of the area. On the contrary,
the Government’s policy all along has been to retain the nominated character of the NDMC.
8.20 Time and again, the Ministry of Home Affairs have argued that in the event of
NDMC being made an elected body, composed of Councillors, accountable to the voters, the
Central Government may not be able to influence and ensure compliance of municipal
governance on critical issues. The Ministry feels that Central Government may not be able
to pre-empt the elected local body on critical policy areas. These arguments of the Ministry
are as fallacious as others, inasmuch as Chapter-XXII of the NDMC Act 1994 contains
adequate provisions empowering the Central Government to exercise oversight of the
functioning of NDMC. Thus, Sections 393-398 of the said Act give powers to the Central
Government to require production of documents; inspection; issue of directions and
enforcement thereof; and dissolution of the Council.
Recommendations of Committee
9.0 The Committee has deliberated on the Bill at length. However, on the question of
making NDMC an elected body, rather than a nominated body as at present, the Committee
26Balakrishnan Report on Reorganisation of Delhi Set-up, Part-II, p. 15

31
is divided. There is no consensus in the Committee either in favour of or against the Bill.
A section of the Members are of the view that the Bill should be passed in its present form.
The other section of the Members strongly feel that keeping in view the spirit of the
Constitution (Seventy-Third Amendment) Act, 1992, the Constitution (Seventy-Fourth
Amendment) Act, 1992, the structure of the Cantonment Boards and the aspirations of the
residents of the NDMC area, the Council should be made into an elected body, at least
partially, on the lines of the Cantonment Boards, to subserve the core principles of local
self governance as enshrined in the Constitution.
9.1 The issue of revolving Chairmanship of the NDMC, for the purpose of presiding over
the meetings of the Council, repeatedly came up for discussion in the Committee. The
majority view in the Committee disagreed with the concept of revolving Chairmanship.
9.2 Be that as it may be, in view of the divergent perception in the Committee on the
subject matter of the Bill, and the persistent stand of the Government of making no change
in the governance structure of NDMC, the Committee is of the considered view that the
Government should take up the issue at the larger level with major political parties and
other stakeholders to reconcile the differing viewpoints and to explore the possibility of
evolving a consensus on this issue, before piloting the Bill in Parliament.

(i) NDMC consists of about 3% of area and 3% of population of the NCT of Delhi. It

(ii) In view of special characteristics of the area, governance based on conventional
pattern of representative self Government was found unworkable. Accordingly, a
special legislation, namely, the New Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994 has been
structured for New Delhi area.
(iii) The composition of the NDMC, as per the existing law is following:
• The Chairperson of the NDMC would be an officer of Central Government or
Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi (GNCTD), not below the rank
of Joint Secretary to the Government of India- to be nominated by the Central
Government in consultation with the Chief Minister of Delhi.
• Three MLAs of Delhi Legislative Assembly representing New Delhi area.
• Five officers of the Central Government or GNCTD.
• Two members from various fields to be nominated by the Central Government in
consultation with Chief Minister of Delhi.
• MP representing New Delhi area as special invitee.
• At least three women members.
• At least one SC member.
• A Vice Chairperson from amongst non-official members to be nominated by the
Central Government in consultation with the Chief Minister, Delhi.

that the Bill contains mainly the following proposals:
(i) To reduce the number of MLAs from three to two and increase the number of
members belonging to various categories like lawyers, teachers, businessmen etc. from
two to four.
(ii) To make the MP representing New Delhi area as Member of the Council with voting
rights.
(iii) At least, two Members should be from SC, of which at least one should be from non-
official category.
(iv) The procedure for presiding over meetings of the Council has also been changed.

3.0 The Chairman welcomed the Home Secretary, the Chairman, NDMC and other senior

3.1 The Home Secretary stated that he had consulted the Union Home Minister on the issues
related to the Bill and the views of the Government of India are as follows:
• The NDMC area has unique characteristics of being the seat of the Central Government
which houses Parliament, Rashtrapati Bhavan, Supreme Court of India, the residences
of Prime Minister, all Central Ministers, MPs, Judges of Supreme Court, Government
Officers.
• There are only a few private colonies in the NDMC area.
• Eighty per cent of the area comprises of Government colony buildings.
• Out of the population of 302360, 220000 are residing in Government colonies and
71,000 are residing in private colonies, including about 12,000 in jhuggies and temporary
huts and about 11,000 in the diplomatic and restricted areas.
• Diplomatic missions of foreign countries are also located in the NDMC area.
• Every State has its Resident Commissioner in the capital and all State Bhavans are
located in the NDMC area.

47
• The Central Government has, therefore, to strike a fine balance between adopting a
system of governance that takes care of the rights of the residents as also the rights
of the foreign missions.
• Implementation of policy decisions taken by locally elected body in the NDMC area may
have a far reaching impact, even impacting the country’s reputation at the international
level.
• The Government servants and their families residing in the Government colonies located
in the NDMC area are in majority. Thus, the Government does not want politicization
of Government officials and their families.
• The amendments which have been proposed in the present Bill are, basically, three. The
first one is with regard to reducing the number of MLAs from three to two due to
delimitation. The second one is to increase the number of nominated Members from two
to four. And the third one is that the MP representing the New Delhi area has been given
full-fledged Membership with voting rights because it has been found that the Chief
Minister, who is currently an MLA from that region, and the local MPs, are not
attending the meetings, partly because they feel that they do not enjoy proper status in
NDMC.
• There are private colonies like JK Dutt Colony, Golf Links, etc in the NDMC area. The
Government is devising mechanism to give representation to the sparsely distributed
private population.
• The view finally taken at the level of the Union Home Minister is that the Government
would, at the moment, still prefer to stick to the amendments and not to make any
further changes in the proposed Bill.

• There is a contradiction in the argument put forward by the Government. The

9.0  The Chair and Members of the Committee while expressing unhappiness over the rigid

7.0 Members then expressed the following views both in favour of and against the Bill.
Against the Bill
■ The Committee should stress upon the point that NDMC should be an elected body and
that the citizens could not be denied their civic rights and responsibilities.
■ While making structural changes in the NDMC, the model of the Cantonment Boards
should be kept in mind wherein there were components of both elected and nominated
members.
■ The functioning of Legislators, MPs and MLAs was completely different from the duties
and responsibilities of a corporator.
■ The post of the Chairman, NDMC ought not be a revolving one. In case the Chairman,
NDMC was not present, there could be a Deputy Chairman to preside over the body.
It would not be in order for the Chief Minister or for that matter a Minister of the
Central Government to preside over the NDMC only because of protocol requirements.
■ The O.M. dated 13 th January, 2011 of the Ministry of Home Affairs attributed negative
motives to a body whose composition was under discussion.
■ There could not be a body which was not answerable to the people. The residents must
have a say in the functioning of NDMC, particularly on civic matters.
■ It was interesting to note that the written submissions of Ministry of Home Affairs
sent to the Committee, spelling out the Government stand on the governing structure
of NDMC, were strikingly identical to the speeches of the then Home Minister in
both the Houses of Parliament during the debates in both the Houses on the NDMC
Bill, 1994.
■ If NDMC was not made an elected body then at least its name should be changed to
‘New Delhi Municipal Board’.
In favour of the Bill
■ Keeping in view, the special character of NDMC area, the amendments proposed in the
Bill should be accepted in the public interest.
■ The Bill was more in the nature of making procedural changes necessitated by recent
developments and protocol requirements and providing additional representation in the
body, which were steps in the right direction.
■ The issue of direct election should not be used as a ploy to derail the passing of the
proposed amendments and in effect inhibiting reform measures proposed for the NDMC.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
The New Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994 has been enacted
to provide for the establishment of the New Delhi Municipal Council
and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. It
provides, inter alia , there shall be three Members of the Legislative
Assembly of Delhi, whose constituency fall fully or partly in the
New Delhi area, as Members in the New Delhi Municipal Council.
After delimitation of Assembly Constituencies in the National Capital
Territory of Delhi, only two such Assembly Constituencies fall
within the New Delhi area and consequently only two Members of
Legislative Assembly may become the members in the New Delhi
Municipal Council.
2. Presently, the Member of Parliament representing the New
Delhi area in the Lok Sabha is a Special Invitee to the meetings of
the New Delhi Municipal Council without voting rights. The
Estimates Committee of Fourteenth Lok Sabha in its Eleventh and
Thirteenth Reports recommended, inter alia , that the Member of
Parliament should be given voting rights.
3. In view of the aforesaid, it is proposed to amend the New
Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994 to provide, inter alia , that,—
(a) the Member of Parliament representing the New
Delhi area in the Lok Sabha shall be made a member of the
New Delhi Municipal Council with voting rights;
(b) the number of members of the Legislative Assembly,
who are members of the Council, be reduced from three to two;
(c) the number of Members representing certain fields
be increased from two to four;
(d) out of thirteen members there shall be at least three
members who are women and two members belonging to the
Scheduled Castes in the Council, out of which one shall be
from the nominated Members representing certain fields.
4. In view of proposed inclusion of the Member of
Parliament, referred to in sub-paragraph ( a) of the preceding
paragraph, in the New Delhi Municipal Council and two Members of
Legislative Assembly being the members of the New Delhi Municipal
Council, it is further proposed to amend the aforesaid Act to revise
the procedure for presiding over the meetings of the Council.
3. This Bill seeks to achieve the above object.

January 13, 2011
Respected Sir,
Our Committee has been discussing in the last 3-4 meetings a proposal to amend the NDMC Act
1994. The amending Bill provides for that:
(i) The Member of Parliament representing the New Delhi area in the Lok Sabha shall be
made a Member of the New Delhi Municipal Council with voting rights;
(ii) The number of Members of the Legislative Assembly, who are members of the
Council, be reduced from three to two. This has been necessitated because of the
reduction of the number of Assembly Constituencies in the NDMC area from three to
two in the recent delimitation;
(iii) The number of Members representing certain fields be increased from two to four; and
(iv) Out of thirteen Members, there shall be at least three Members who are women and
two Members belonging to the Scheduled Castes in the Council, out of which one
shall be from nominated Members representing certain fields.
(v) To provide for an order of precedence in presiding over the meetings of the NDMC.
It is being provided for that if the Chief Minister is a Member and attends the meeting,
the Chief Minister will preside over the meeting; failing that, if a Member of Parliament
and Minister in the Government of India is a Member and attends the meeting, he/she
will preside over the meeting; failing that, if a member of Parliamment is a Member
and attends the meeting, he/she will preside over the meeting. In all other cases, the
Chairperson will continue to chair the meeting of the council as at present.
The proposed amendments seek to broad base the representative character of the NDMC.
Sir, I have gone through various papers relating to the demand for an elective body to replace the
NDMC in the past. However, it may be observed that the various Committees which have gone
into this issue on earlier occasions have persisted with the present setup in the larger interest of
maintaining a distinct character of this area.

Dear Venkaiah Ji,
With reference to discussions held in the previous meetings of the Committee on proposal
to amend the NDMC Act, 1994, and the final reply of the Home Ministry on the said subject matter
along with the relevant valuable extracts and documents provided by the secretariat, I have come
to the following conclusions,
(1) As far as voting right to the Member of Parliament representing the New Delhi area is
concerned, it was stated that he/she has never been able to participated in the meeting of
the Council, I think a person loaded with such a huge amount of official & social
responsibilities can not be expected to sit in the council’s meeting as idle or mere
inoperative. I am fully agree with the other member’s suggestion that such Member of
Parliament should be made empowered with the voting right, so that he will have some
stake in the functioning and decision making of the Council and would feel accountable to
his duties as a member of the Council as well.
(2) Considering the distinctive character of the area fall in the jurisdiction of the NDMC as it
is also a seat of Central Government in the Union of India, not many changes can be made
in the amending Bill. Though, the reply of the Home Ministry seems to be more
bureaucratic than democratic. It should be made quite clear that there is a vast difference
between administered and empowered. The aspirations and democratic representation of the
residents can not be denied irrespective of the provisions given by any specific exception.
Though, it, keeps a very distinguished and unique ingredients of national and international
importance, NDMC can not be converted in to a fully democratically elected body in
one sweep but its composition can be adjusted suited to the aspiration and
representation of the people of the area for now. Therefore,
(a) In the light of the available options and the substantial amount of population and its
character, fall in the jurisdiction area of NDMC, I opine that the two nominated
members among the RW As should be accommodated in the Council , but it
should also be ensured that these members have elected democratically in their
respective associations and all the RW As should be given equal opportunity.

Chairman and Vice Chairman each appointed by the Central Government in
consultation with the Chief minister of Delhi, one Member of Parliament, two
MLAs, two representatives of RW As and as proposed, four persons of various
nominated in consultation with the Government of NCT will constitute more than
an absolute majority in favor of  the direct and indirect representation of the residents

1.1. IMPLEMENTATION OF NER PROJECTS 
 
Recommendation 
1.1.1 Human beings have little or no control o ver the vagaries of weather. Likewise, the 
climatic peculiarities of the North-East are not new and cannot and   should not be used as a 
pretext for the slow pace of utilization of f unds and delayed completions of projects in the 
NER. Therefore, given the climat ic conditions of that region, it would be a prudent step on 
the part of administrative Minist ry and the State Governments, to organize the activities in a 
rational way to offset the adverse impact of th e nature. Accordingly, the projects in NER 
should be implemented during the seasons when conditions are favourable, at a grater pace, 
to compensate the loss of time during the mons oon season, so that projects are implemented 
in time. In this context, the Committee would like to advise the Government to step up vigil in 
monitoring the expenditure, as in the flurry of works, there is every likelihood of siphoning of 
funds meant for development.  
  (Para 2.1.11)  
Action Taken 
1.1.2 The State Governments have been advised to  plan the implementation of the projects 
in such a way that the adverse impact of na ture could not affect implementation and the 
projects may be implemented with greater p ace during working season to compensate the 
loss of time during monsoon season. The State Gove rnments have also been advised to keep 
in view the workload available with various executing agencies in the State taking into 
account the capacity of indivi dual executing agency while proposing the projects in the 
annual priority list so as to distribute the equal workload to all the executing agencies.   
 
1.1.3 To encourage the States for timely comp letion of projects it has been decided to 
provide an incentive to good performing Stat es in terms of completion of projects by 
retaining projects upto Rs.20.00 cr ore as per State’s choice over and above its annual 
entitlement.     
 
1.1.4 To strengthen the monitoring of the projec ts the Ministry instructed designated State-
wise Area Officers for making bi -monthly visits to the States  for review of the NLCPR 
Scheme and field visits to the project sites. Ch ief Secretaries of the St ates have been advised 
for holding regular quarterly meetings on the scheme.  
 
Further Observation 
1.1.5 The Committee, while noting the reply, desires to be informed of the steps taken 
by the State Governments in this regard and the impact thereof.

3.6.1 The Committee is of the view that to ma ke any project successful in terms of

INTRODUCTION 
  I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, 
having been authorized by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this 
One Hundred and Fiftieth Report on Action Taken by Government on the 
observations/recommendations contained in the One Hundred and Forty-Fourth Report on Demands 
for Grants (2010-11) of the Ministry of Home Affairs. 
2.  The One Hundred and Forty-Fourth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Home Affairs was presented to the Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of the Lok Sabha 
on 27th April, 2010. 
3.  The Ministry of Home Affairs furnished the Action Taken Replies on the One Hundred and 
Forty Fourth Report. The Minister of Home Affairs laid on the Table of the Lok Sabha the status of 
implementation of recommendations contained in the said report of the Committee, on 23rd 
November, 2010 pursuant to the direction of the Chairman, Rajya Sabha and presented the same in the 
Rajya Sabha on 24th November, 2010. 
4.  The Committee considered the draft Report an d adopted the same at its meeting held on 15 
April, 2011. 
5.  The recommendations/observations of the Committee are printed in bold letters. 
 
 
 
  M. VENKAIAH NAIDU
 
NEW DELHI; Chairman, 
15th April, 2010 Department-related Parliamentary 
  Standing Committee on Home Affairs

of Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha on the 27th April, 2010.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
1.1  Modernisation of State Police Forces (MPF) 
Recommendation 
1.1.1 The Committee is of the considered view that the Scheme is of utmost importance so far as the 
maintenance of law and order in the States is concerned. Therefore, the earmarked provision for the 
Scheme must be utilized fully and optimally. In this connection, active participation of State 
Governments is necessary. The Committee, therefor e, impresses upon the State Governments that 
Utilization Certificates may be submitted in time so that they could avail of the funds under the 
Scheme. The Committee takes a serious view of the fact that even some of the States affected by left 
wing extremism are not properly availing the Scheme. Such States have not submitted the UCs for 
2007-08 which would obviously deprive them in getting their full share of funds in future. The 
Committee finds it disturbing that on one side, the State are reeling under the impact of left wing 
extremism, as shown by the recent example of the Dantewada incident on 6.4.2010, in which a large 
number of security personnel were but chered by the ultras. On the hand, the affected States display 
lack of interest in availing of the Scheme. The Committee desires that the Minister of Home Affairs 
should discuss the matters with all the concerned Chief Ministers. (Para 3.1.12 of 144th Report) 
Action Taken 
1.1.2  The issue would be discussed in the next Conference of Chief Ministers on Internal Security. 
Further Recommendation 
1.1.3  The Committee may be informed of the decisi ons taken in the last Conference of Chief 
Ministers on Internal Security. 
Recommendation 
1.1.4  The Committee appreciates introduction of the system of Concurrent Audit to monitor timely 
and appropriate use of the funds sanctioned and released under the MPF Scheme. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs should apprise it of the highlights as well as the 
corrective steps contemplated in the light of the Action Taken Reports received from the State 
Governments. (Para 3.1.13 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.1.5  The quarterly concurrent audit of utilization of MPF funds by States is being conducted by the 
Departmental Accounting Organization of Ministry of Home Affairs. The quarterly concurrent audit 
reports as and when received are being forwarded to concerned States for taking remedial action and 
furnish action taken reports (ATRs) to the Ministry. These ATRs are taken into consideration while 
considering release of funds to the States. Some of the common issues which have been noticed in the 
concurrent audit reports are as under: 

(i) The funds released by the Central Gove rnment are not being used by the State 
Governments within the financial year itself. In some cases, funds are used for items not 
included in the plan approved by the Ministry. 
(ii) State Governments are not incurring timely expenditure out of their own share under the 
scheme. 
(iii) The procurement and installation of equipm ent is taking long time. Therefore, the audit 
is asking for speeding of the process. The period between initiation of tender process and 
its finalization is long in many cases.  
(iv) Most of the State Governments are not maintaining stock registers of items purchased 
under the MPF scheme. 
(v) The State Governments are not releasing funds in time to Police Departments which is 
resulting in delay in the modernization process. 
(vi) Where the buildings are complete, the St ate Government is delaying the process of 
giving the building to the police for proper use. 
(vii) Forensic science laboratories are not optimally using the facilities due to lack of 
manpower. 
(viii) The training infrastructure is not being fully developed and in some cases calendar of 
training is not available. 
(ix) Expenditure statements from field units are not reaching PHQs in time as a result they 
are not able to furnish UCs to the Ministry in time. 
(x) In some States, there are no monitoring comm ittees to review the progress of work under 
MPF. 
(xi) In cases where procurement of weapons and equipment had been completed, no action 
has been taken to put them to immediate use. 
1.1.6  As already stated above, the audit reports are being sent to respective States with the request to 
furnish ATRs to MHA. The submission of ATRs on concurrent audit report is linked to release of 
Central funds to States. It is expected that in due course of time the system would improve to the 
satisfaction of audit requirement. 
Further Recommendation 
1.1.7  The Committee appreciates the fact that the Au dit Reports are sent by the Ministry of 
Home Affairs to respective States with the request to furnish ATRs. But the Committee is 
disturbed to note the inconsistencies and deficiencies that are there in the common issues 
identified by the Ministry in the ATRs. The Mi nistry should make it compulsory for all the 
States to take corrective measu res on all these deficiencies, a nd if necessary, at the Minister’s 
level the issues may be taken up with the Chief Ministers. 
Recommendation 

1.1.8 The Committee, while appreciating the laying of more focus on the components of operational 
buildings such as police stations, police outposts and police lines as a part of effective budgeting for 
Annual Action Plan of States under the Modernizatipn of Police Forces, feels that earmarking Rs. 
2.00 crore per district for naxal affected Districts, is meagre. Keeping in view the use of latest 
weapons by the outlaws and their strategy to attack police establishments, the allocation and facilities 
to police establishments and personnel should be appropriately increased. However, this should not 
be done across the board and should be linked to utilization.   
Action Taken 
1.1.9 The Ministry, prima-facie, agrees with the recommendation of the Parliamentary Committee. 
The MPF Scheme was approved by the Cabinet upto the year 2009-10 in the year 2000. In view of the 
demands of States for its continuation for another 5-10 years, the CCS has approved the proposal of 
the Ministry for extension of the scheme for one year i.e. 2010-11 pending the study of the Scheme by 
BPR&D in order to enable the Government to take a decision on its further continuation for another 5-
10 years and suggestions/recommendations to be incorporated in the new/revised Scheme. One of the 
TORs for the study by BPR&D was about requiremen t of NE States, J&K and naxal affected States. 
In the light of this position, the implementation is dependent upon the decision of the Government to 
continue the scheme for another 5-10 years beyond 2010-11 based on the assessment of BPR&D. As 
for the current financial year i.e, 2010-11, the Scheme has been extended, on as is where is basis; no 
change in the amount of Rs.2 crore for naxal affected districts has been made. It may, however, be 
noted here that as against 31 Naxal affected Districts supported in 2008-09, 51 Districts were 
supported in 2009-10 under the Scheme and during the current financial year, 83 Naxal affected 
Districts are being supported. 
1.2 CIVIL DEFENCE 
Recommendation 
1.2.1 The Committee has made detailed recommendations in its One Hundred and Thirty-sixth 
Report on the Revamping and Revitalization of Civil Defence in the country and it intends to present 
an Action Taken Report thereon, which would contain detailed observations and recommendations in 
the light of action taken by the Government. Since the Government is revamping the Civil Defence set 
up, fund requirements may be assessed properly. Regular monitoring on the revamping may be made. 
Enrolling young and active volunteers should be made a regular feature. The total volunteer force 
should also be trained in disaster management. The Committee urges upon the Government to create 
awareness amongst all citizens for the imperative need to discharge their fundamental duties, to 
uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of the country and to defend the country and 
render national service when called upon to do so. The Committee also urges upon the Government to 
prepare detailed plans to provide training to all able-bodied citizens so that they can perform their 
fundamental duties. (Para 3.2.7 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.2.2 The assessment of requirement of funds for various components of the Revamping of Civil 
Defence Scheme in the country has been made on the basis of the recommendations of the Committee 
headed by Shri K.M. Singh, Member NDMA. 

1.2.3 The Scheme for Revamping of Civil Defence, set up in the country at a cost of Rs.l 00 crore, is 
under implementation. The scheme is being regularly monitored at various levels. 
1.2.4 The officers of the Civil Defenee at the level of Dy. Controllers have been sensitized about the 
important aspects of the scheme and have been provided with practical solutions to the problems being 
faced by the State Civil Defence Staff at the ground level. 
1.2.5 In order to enroll young and active volunteers in Civil Defence force, an intensive drive was 
undertaken across all the States to weed out the inactive, old and infirm volunteers and to enroll new 
energetic volunteers. The process has since been completed by the States/UTs, in the month of May 
2010, after screening all volunteers. A total of 57,939 volunteers have been weeded out and 39,708 
new volunteers have been enrolled after the launch of the Scheme. The process of further enrolling 
young and active volunteers is in progress in the States/UTs. 
1.2.6 As part of Pilot Project to sensitize the volunteers in the field of Disaster Management, about 
212 Master Trainers had been trained in Disaster Management Skills in addition to Internal Security 
duties at National Civil Defence College, Nagpur. These Master Trainers have further imparted 
training to 1875 volunteers, till date, at State Level. The training of volunteers will continue for the 
next few months till the whole target of training 4280 volunteers is fully achieved. Financial support 
of procurement of Disaster Management equipments , creation of infrastructure and transport to 100 
selected Multi Hazard Prone Districts through DGCD is being extended. 
1.2.7 As per the recommendations of the Second Administrative Reforms Commission, 1% 
population of the country has to be brought under the fold of Civil Defence. Under the scheme of 
Revamping the Civil Defence, provision has been made for awareness and publicity. It is expected 
that the steps taken would go a long way to facilitate creation of awareness among the citizens of this 
country about their role in rendering national services when eventuality so arises. 
1.3 NATIONAL DISASTER MANAGEMENT 
Recommendation 
1.3.1 The Committee understands the need for strengthening mitigation, preparedness and response 
measures for effective and efficient management of natural as well as manmade disasters keeping in 
view vulnerable geo-climatic conditions, of the country such as 58.6% earthquake prone landmass, 
12% area floods prone and 68% cultivable area drought prone.  The Committee, however, observes 
that most of the new programmes/ augmentation of on going programmes are at the rudimentary 
stages. It would take considerable time for the new programmes to take of. The Committee is 
constrained to note that even though the Act was passed in 2005, there is no perceptible improvement 
in the disaster management preparedness in the country. The 26/11 terrorist attack in Mumbai is a 
glaring example when it took a lot of time for the NSG commandoes to reach the spot. There are 
several instances of handling of major fires, floods/droug hts and major accidents, including recently 
radioactive leakages (Cobalt 60), which should have been tackled with great promptness and 
effectively. The Committee therefore, urges upon the Ministry of Home Affairs and NDMA to take this 
task as a major challenge so that tangible results are visible for the countrymen. National Institute of 
Disaster Management is functioning from rented premises. Land/Buildings for three battalions of 
NDRF are yet to be acquired. Though Phase I of National Emergency Communication Plan has been 

completed, the Committee apprehends that the provision of a meagre amount of Rs. 10 crore is not 
sufficient in view of the vastness of the country and its vulnerability. Therefore, fund requirements 
need to be re-assessed. The Committee also recommends that 124 posts sanctioned for the NDMA may 
be filled up at the earliest. There should not be any delay in this regard. (Para 3.3.4 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.3.2 In view of the vulnerability of several part s of this country and geo climatic conditions, a 
Central Act i.e. Disaster Management Act, 2005 was enacted. This Act paved the way for creation of 
NDMA with core function to lay down policies, plans and guidelines for disaster management for 
ensuring timely and effective response to disaster s. NDMA has since then released several specific 
guidelines on management of earthquake, floods, cyclones, biological disasters, chemical (industrial) 
disaster, chemical (terrorism) disaster, nuclear and radiological emergencies, psycho-social support 
and preparation of State Disaster Management Plans etc. Several other guidelines on the subject are in 
the process of its conceptualization & formulation. 
1.3.3 In addition, NDMA has been generating awareness on preparedness through print and 
electronic media and organizing mock drills. NDMA is also in the process of formulation of several 
Mitigation Projects such as National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project, National Earthquake Risk 
Mitigation Project, National Flood Mitigation Project, National Landslide Risk Mitigation Project. 
1.3.4 The National Policy on Disaster Management (NDPM) has been placed on the website of 
NDM Division of MHA. The Policy covers all aspects of disaster management covering institutional, 
legal and financial arrangements; disaster prevention, mitigation and preparedness; techno-legal 
regime; response; relief and rehabilitation; reconstruction and recovery; capacity development; 
knowledge management and research and development. It focuses on the areas where action is needed 
and the institutional mechanism through which such action can be channelized. 
1.3.5 As far as the incidence regarding radiation from Cobalt (60) which occurred in Mayapuri area 
of Delhi during April, 2010 is concerned, it was dealt/responded promptly by an expert team of 
NDMA comprising of CBRN trained NDRF. Severity of radioactivity was assessed in the patients 
admitted in the hospital and they were advised/administered suitable medical care. The mechanism to 
deal such kind of disaster is being developed and expected to be institutionalized in due course. 
1.3.6 National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) has been constituted with 8 battalions, as a 
specialist force to respond to disaster or disaster like situation. So far NDRF have undertaken to rescue 
lives of more than 21000 persons in different States including relief supply, medical aid, medicines 
and drinking water. 
1.3.7 The matter for allotment of land for NIDM for developing its own campus has been taken up 
with the DDA, New Delhi. Allocation of requisite fund has already been made in Budget. Effort is on 
to solve the problem of land availability. 
1.3.8 Similarly, the issue of acquiring land for National Disaster Response Force battalions has been 
taken up in right earnest. Land has been made available for six Battalions of NDRF viz. at Kolkata, 
Ghaziabad, Arakkonam, Mundali, Gandhinagar and Pune. For the other two battalions, efforts are on 
to make the land available. Further infrastructure is being built on the land acquired for those six 
battalions. 

1.3.9 The amount of Rs.10 crore provided for Ph ase-II of the National Emergency Communication 
Plan is only a token provision. A plan proposal in consultation with NIC, Department of Space and 
NDRF is under formulation and accordingly additional funds will be sought. 
1.3.10  NDMA has been given sanction of 124 posts of Secretariat Staff against which 73 posts have 
been filled up. Besides that, NDMA has engaged 16 consultants and outsourced 90 people for 
different works. 
Further Recommendation 
1.3.11 The Committee desires that the guidelines on  the subjects, which are at the stages of 
conceptualization and formulation, may be given final shape at the earliet and an early solution 
may be found to the problem of  land availability since requisi te fund had been made in the 
Budget. 
1.4 HOME GUARDS 
Recommendation 
1.4.1 The Committee appreciates the role played by the Home Guards in assisting police in 
maintaining law & order and in various other security related duties including disaster management. 
The Committee agrees with the suggestions made by second ARC. In the present day scenario, 
disaster management and para medical training are very important and these should be made an 
integral part of the training of Home Guards. The Committee is however given to understand that the 
picture is not so rosy as it is being projected. Home Guard Jawans do not receive the needed moral 
support, proper leadership and financial incentives. They are always under the feeling of job 
insecurity and are inducted mostly on part-time basis. The Committee is unhappy to note that the 
States are not submitting their claims on time and therefore allocation is getting reduced and so is the 
expenditure which also gets reduced reluctantly. It is an unfortunate situation where States are not 
properly making use of the scheme and the funds. The centre should write to all the States to 
implement the scheme in letter and spirit and make their claims on a regular basis. The Committee 
recommends that the Union Home Minister may ta ke up this issue with all the State Governments 
impressing upon them the need to make optimum use of the scheme, submit claims regularly so that 
adequate funds could be allocated and released A review of the role and responsibilities of Home 
Guards may be undertaken to revitalize their role and consequent augmentation of the resources.(Para 3.4.8 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.4.2 Home Guard volunteers are raised under Home  Guards Acts/Rules enacted by the respective 
State Governments/UT Administrations. Central Government makes guidelines/policy for proper 
functioning of Home Guards Organization in various States/UTs. ‘Home Guards’ being a State 
subject, its implementation is carried out by the States/UTs. 
1.4.3 The proposal to increase the duty/training al lowance of Home Guards from Rs.45/- to Rs.250/- 
is under consideration of the Government. This will enhance the morale of  Home Guards volunteers 
and also result in attracting better quality of manpower to this organization. 
1.4.4 During last three years  i.e. 2007-08, 2008-09 and 2009-10, Rs.48.00 crore, Rs.46.527 crore and 
Rs.44.l415 crore, respectively, have been sanction ed for re-imbursement to the States. However, the 
States are regularly being advised by DG, Civil Defence to submit all outstanding claims of previous 

years along with audit certificates. State Governme nts are being advised by the Ministry of Home 
Affairs to expeditiously and regularly submit their reimbursement claims. This will facilitate optimum 
utilization of the allocated funds and will result in efficient implementation of the Scheme. 
 
... 
Further Recommendation 
1.4.5 The Committee welcomes the proposal and rec ommends that a decision in the matter of 
increasing duty/training allowance may be taken at the earliest. 
1.5 FIRE SERVICES 
Recommendation 
1.5.1 The Committee having taken note of the major fire accidents with alarming regularity in the 
country, causing heavy causalties, particularly in commercial buildings in Bangalore and the 
Stephen’s Court Building in Kolkata, wishes to highlight the weaknesses in the fire fighting 
mechanism of the country. The Committee notes with dismay that lessons have not been learnt from 
the heart-rendering incidents of Dabwali (1995) Kumbakonam (2004), and Uphaar Cinema, (Delhi) 
(1997) tragedies. The National Building Code (NBC) published in 1970 and updated in 2005 does 
prescribe the minimum fire safety and rescue measures to be provided in the buildings but what is 
missing is the actual enforcement mechanism. Transparency in giving clearance to construction of 
structures must be in place and public access to building safety data, a practice common in other 
parts of the world, ought to adopted in our country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
Government must undertake required steps for strengthening of fire fighting mechanism. The old and 
the new structures should comply with the mandated rules and the State Governments must be 
persuaded to ensure enforcement and compliance of the fire fighting measures and safety code. The 
Committee also recommends that a complete overhauling of fire services needs on an emergent basis 
be done. The Committee takes a serious note of the fact that the allocation of Rs. 38 crore made at BE 
2009-10 was reduced to Rs. 14 crore at RE. This needs to be seriously looked into. (Para 3.5.6 ibid)  
Action Taken 
1.5.2 It is primarily for the State Governments to ensure safety of life and property from fire related 
accidents as Fire Service is a State subject and has been included as a muni cipal function in the XII 
Schedule of the Constitution of India in terms of Article 243- W. Ministry plays an advisory role by 
issuing fire safety guidelines as recommended by Standing Fire Advisory Council, an apex advisory 
body, constituted by the Government of India, Ministry of Home Affairs. 
1.5.3 State Governments are also being assisted to get monetary assistan ce as soft loans from 
General Insurance Corporation and Grants-in-Aid as per recommendations of Finance Commissions. 
As per recommendations of X and XI Finance Commissions, Rs.686 crore (approximately) were 
provided for the development of Fire Service in the country. 
1.5.4 In the XIth Plan, Rs.200 crore has been allocated for the Centrally Sponsored Scheme – -
”Strengthening of Fire & Emergency Services”. Un der this Scheme, State Fi re Services shall be 

strengthened by providing them Advanced Water Tenders, High Pressure Pumps with water mist 
technology and Quick Response Vehicles. 
1.5.5 Further, Fire Risk and Hazard Analysis in th e country will also be undertaken for the first time 
for preparing a Fire Service preparedness plan for the country. 
1.5.6 As far as reduction of fund in 2009-10 at RE  is concerned, the fact is this that Budgetary 
provision against this scheme sanctioned for Rs.200 crore have started flowing to the States since 
financial year 2009-10. Since the scheme was approved only after passage of more than 6 months in 
that financial year i.e. during October 2009, the allocation was reduced to Rs.14 crore in the Revised 
Estimate. However, in the current financial year (2010-11), the allocated amount of Rs.38 crore is 
expected to be fully utilized and also further efforts are being made to step up the financial provision. 
1.5.7 Also, Ministry has considered the proposal for improvement of training standards of Fire 
Service personnel in the country. Accordingly an amount of Rs.205 crore in Non-Plan has been 
approved for the period 2010-2013 for upgradation of National Fire Service College, Nagpur. 
1.5.8 As stated above, Standing Fire Advisory Council has already recommended for adopting the 
Fires Safety Guidelines, as contained in the National Building Code of India. Compendium of 
Instruction of Standing Fire Advisory Council, containing these guidelines and recommendations, 
have been circulated to all concerned for implementation.Actual implementation rest with the local bodies /  
State Government. 
1.5.9 Further, following recommendations of the 13th Finance Commission have been accepted by 
the Central Government and accordingly funds will be available for meeting the requirement of Fire & 
Emergency Services in the country – 
(i) Finance Commission has allocated Rs.87519 crore to the local bodies. A portion of the 
grant provided to the urban local bodies will be spent on revamping of Fire Services 
within their respective jurisdictions. The State will be eligible to draw its share only if 
they comply with nine conditions out of which one of the conditions in "All Municipal 
Corporations with a population of more than  1 million (2001 census) must put in place a 
fire hazard response and mitigation plan for their respective jurisdictions. Publication of 
these plans in the respective State Government gazettes will demonstrate compliance 
with this condition". 
(ii) In addition, Rs.472 crore to the 7 Stat es namely Andhra Pradesh (Rs.17 crore), Haryana 
(Rs.100 crare), Mizoram (Rs.20 crore), Ori ssa (Rs.150 crore), Tripura (Rs.15 crore), 
Uttar Pradesh (Rs.20 crore only for Varanasi) and West Bengal (Rs.150 crore) have been 
allocated for revamping of Fire & Emergency Services. 
Further Recommendation 
1.5.10  The Committee feels that role of the Cent ral Government does not end up with 
providing monetary assistance and grant-in-aid on the plea that the Fire Services is a State 
subject. The Apex Council needs to be strengthe ned to make its presence felt. Though the 
code/Rules/Manuals/Regulations exist on paper, their actual enforcement and transparency in 
giving fire safety clearance in construction of structures , are lacking. The Committee takes note 

of reported fire and safety clearance given to so me guest houses in Gurgaon before completion 
of construction activities. Such irregularities need to be curbed with firm hands. The Committee 
also desires that the upgradatio n of National Fire Service college , Nagpur be taken up in time 
bound manner. 
1.6 NAXALISM 
Recommendation 
1.6.1 It is an admitted fact that the implementation of various schemes, particularly of the Ministry 
of Rural Development and the Ministry of Tribal Affairs, is deficient and there is no proper 
administrative control and monitoring which obviously lead to dissatisfaction among the people and 
they fall easy prey to the extremists. Efforts, therefore, should be made in the direction of 
implementing the flagship programmes in a proper manner to ensure that the beneficiaries feel part of 
the mainstream of the society. 
(Para 4.10.4 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.6.2 The Ministry of Rural Development implements various schemes through State Governments 
and UT Administrations. A comprehensive Monitoring Mechanism is under implementation to 
monitor the implementation of the programmes, including utilization of funds through Periodical 
Progress Reports, Performance Review Committee Meetings, Area Officer’s Scheme, Vigilance and 
Monitoring Committees at the State and District levels and National Level Monitors to monitor 
quality of work and adherence to implementation of schemes as per programme guidelines. 
1.6.3 The State Governments and Union Territory Administrations have been advised to adopt a five 
- pronged strategy to improve the functioning of the rural development schemes consisting of (i) 
creation of awareness about the schemes, (ii) transparency, (iii) people’s participation (iv) 
accountability, social audit and (v) vigilance and m onitoring of rural development programmes at all 
levels. 
1.6.4 The Ministry of Tribal Affairs has taken note of the suggestions of the Committee for 
compliance. Regular attention is being given to improve performance. 
Recommendation 
1.6.5 The Government should identify the factors responsible for tardy implementation of the 
schemes and ensure that its benefits reach the targeted groups and they do not feel alienated. In this 
context, the Government should address the issues related to land acquisition, landalienation, 
resettlement and rehabilitation; issues pertaining to laws applicable to the scheduled and tribal areas, 
on priority. The Committee would also like to highlight the fact that in some States elections are not 
held regularly to the Panchayats and other local bodies, which results in lack of participation of 
peoples’ representatives in the implementation of the flagship programmes. It is therefore, equally 
important that elections are held regularly to the P RI Institutions so that public representatives are 
actively involved at the grass root level in implementation of the schemes and projects which would 
directly help in bringing the people back to the mainstream. (Para 4.10.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 

1.6.6 Government of India brought out National Rehabilitation & Resettlement Policy 2007 so that 
people affected due to land acquisition or otherwise are provided with adequate livelihood option and 
other facilities. Keeping in view the various problem s faced by the displaced person, particularly the 
tribal people, Ministry of Rural Development had introduced Land Acquisition (Amendment) Bill and 
Rehabilitation & Resettlement Bill 2009 which was passed by the Lok Sabha but was not taken up in 
Rajya Sabha in the year 2009. However, the Bills lapsed with dissolution of 14th Lok Sabha. 
Thereafter, in consultation with Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs, the process is on to re-introduce the 
Land Acquisition (Amendment) Bill and Rehabilitation & Resettlement Bill. The Bills which were 
introduced in 2009 had specific provision to protec t the interests of tribals. These two laws are 
expected to address the issues causing hardships due to land acquisition and displacement of poor 
people in general and particularly the tribal with specific safeguards for scheduled areas. 
1.6.7 As regards holding elections to the Panchayats , only Jharkhand could not do so because of the 
court case. Supreme Court has since delivered the judgement and the State Government is making 
good efforts to hold Panchayats election at the earliest. 
Recommendation 
1.6.8  The areas affected by LWE are mostly in the central parts of India which has less density of 
population, more density of forest areas; less infrastructure facilities, including education, health and 
roads. It is, therefore, essential that these infrastructure facilities are improved and developed at a 
much faster pace than has been projected and implemented so far. More and more roads are required 
to be built so that it gives employment to jobless people, including tribals while connecting those 
areas with the rest of the country. 
(Para 4.10.6 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.6.9 It is an important mandate of NRHM to ensure availability of health infrastructure like PHCs 
and sub-centres to provide services in the back ward High Focus LWE districts. The States were 
persuaded to substantially increase fund allocation to the high focus districts. This has been ensured in 
PIP of 2010-11 resulting in an increase of allocati on in the LWE district from Rs.271.85 crore in 
2009-10 to Rs.654.61 crore. In 2010-11 (an increase of almost 100% over last year’s allocation). 
Decentralized planning being the cornerstone of NRHM, districts have been allocated these funds as 
per their requirements for improving healthcare services, most important of them being infrastructure 
strengthening. 
1.6.10  The Project Approval Board for SSA has approved the Annual Work Plan & Budget of 35 
Left Wing Extremism (LWE) districts (34 focus districts and West  Medinipur district) for 2010-11. A 
statement on district-wise physical targets agains t the identified indicators and total financial 
allocation under SSA, NPEGEL and KGBV is enclosed as Annexure-I. The total allocation for the 
LWE affected districts has increased by 49% from Rs.2,03,771.84 lakh in 2009-10 to Rs.3,02,865.72 
lakh in 2010-11. The highest increase is in respect of the districts of Kankar (97%) Dantewara (85%), 
Narayanpur (86%) and Bijapur (85%). The physical targets in respect of the identified indicators have 
been approved on the basis of a detailed appraisal of  the requirements projected by the States in their 
district plans. 
1.6.11 The Government on 26.02.2010 has approved scheme for development of 1202 km. National 
Highways and 4363 km. State Roads to two lane standards at an estimated cost of Rs.7300 crore under 

Road Requirement Plan (RRP) in Left Wing Extrem ism (LWE) affected areas of 34 Districts in 8 
States. So far, detailed estimates in respect of 127 works covering a length of 3533 km. costing 
Rs.4074 crore have been sanctioned. Out of thes e 49 works covering a length of 1255 km. costing 
Rs.1437 crore have been awarded. Further, against savings in the approved RRP, proposal for 
inclusion of additional works covering a length of Rs.742.50 km. costing Rs.950 crore is under 
consideration. 
Recommendation 
1.6.12  Education is the basic ingredient of human resource development. Lack of educational 
facilities in the naxal-affected areas is an important factor accountable for the spread of the 
movement. More and more schools with free boarding are required to be opened in the affected areas. 
Vacancies for the posts of teachers may be filled up and to the extent possible, educated youth from 
those areas may be taken as teachers through a special drive. Technical and engineering institutions 
may also be opened in those areas. 
(Para 4.10.7 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.6.13  33 districts affected with Left Wing Extr emism were identified in the year 2009-10 for 
focused attention in the areas of development. An amount of Rs.2,03,771.84 lakh was allocated for the 
implementation of interventions under Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA), KGBV and NPEGEL in the

Rs.1,42,840.02 lakh. Status of district and State-wise physical targets and achievement in respect of 
the identified indicators and financial achievement against the total district-wise allocation for 2009-
10 is enclosed as Annexure-I.  
1.6.14  Later Ramgarh was added in the list of 33 focus district. The Project Approval Board for SSA 
has already approved the Annual Work Plan & Budget of all these 35 districts (34 focus districts and 
West Medinipur district) for 2010-11. A statement on district-wise physical targets against the 
identified indicators and total financial allocation under SSA, NPEGEL and KGBV is enclosed as 
Annexure-II. It can be seen from the Statement at  Annexure-II that the tota l allocation for the LWE 
affected districts has increased by 49% from Rs. 2,03,771.84 lakh in 2009-10 to Rs. 3,02,865.72 lakh 
in 2010-11. The highest increase is in respect of the districts of Kankar (97%), Dantewara (85%), 
Narayanpur (86%) and Bijapur (85%). The physical targets in respect of the identified indicators have 
been approved on the basis of a detailed appraisal of  the requirements projected by the States in their

1.6.16  Drinking water is another basic requirement for the people. In most of the habitations in the 
extremist-affected areas, people do not have access to potable drinking water and even if it is 
available, people, particularly women, have to trek long distances to obtain a pot of water. The 

Government should make use of the existing schemes available and provide drinking water facilities 
in all the habitations by the end of the Eleventh Five-year Plan. (Para 4.10.10 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.6.17  Based on the progress of implementation of Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme 
(ARWSP) so far, the difficulties experienced by the States in its implementation in rural areas and the 
felt need for further refi nement in the programme, the Government of India further modified the 
programme for its implementation in the 11th Five Year Plan period. The revised programme 
rechristened as National Rural Drinking Water Programme (NRDWP), came into vogue with effect 
from 01.04.2009 onwards. The modified programmes’ goal is to provide every household/every 
person, irrespective of the size, with adequate safe water for drinking, cooking and other domestic 
basic needs on a sustainable basis. This basic requirement should meet minimum water quality 
standards and be readily and conveniently accessible at all times and in all situations. 
1.6.18  The norm of 100 persons as the minimum size of a habitation to be covered, has been 
removed with effect from 01.04.2009. All habitation irrespective of the size of the population have to 
be covered under NRDWP. This will benefit small and remote habitations in tribal and forest areas as 
in LWE districts. 
1.6.19  The revised programme gives emphasis on sustainability of sources and systems and 20% of 
the allocation under NRDWP is towards attaining long-term sustainability of water supply to rural 
areas. Further, under the modified programme, priority has been given for coverage of 0% and 0% - 
25% population coverage habitations and quality affected habitations. Thus low coverage areas get 
priority. 
1.6.20  In the allocation of funds to States, 10% weightage has been given to Rural SC/ST population 
in addition to 40% weightage given to overall population of the State, which ensures more funds to 
States with higher SC/ST population which inter alia includes Left Wing Extremism (LWE) affected 
areas. 
1.6.21  States are required to earmark at least 25% of the NRDWP funds for drinking water supply to 
SC dominated habitations and 10% for the ST dominated habitation. 
1.6.22  To give an impetus for implementation of water and sanitation programme in LWE affected 
area, a National Level Workshop on Drinking Water and Sanitation in LWE affected Districts was 
organized on 20-21 January, 2010 in Bhubaneswar, Orissa. The workshop was attended by District 
and State officials and was focused on providing them guidance in drawing up an action plan for IEC 
and Training and two year action plan for ensuring full coverage under Rural Drinking Water and 
Sanitation Programme in these Districts. 
1.6.23  During Annual Plan discussions for 2010-2011, the concerned States have been advised to 
give priority to LWE affected districts by taking up more schemes and investing more funds in these 
districts. 
1.6.24  The funds under NRDWP are released to the States.

up the process in courts and for providing designated judicial services to the litigants. The

MIDDLE 
 CLASS PEOPLE  
Recommendation 
1.7.1 It is a sad state of affairs that no super speciality treatment/services are available in the 
Islands and the people have to travel to Tamil Nadu or Kolkata for treatment for which expenditure is

to the woes of the people in general and its empl oyees particularly the pensioners who are living in 
that Islands. The Committee recommends that Ministry of Home Affairs may take up this matter with

also recommends that the Government should also formulate suitable medical insurance scheme for 
all the persons living in the Islands. 
 (Para 5.3.2 ibid)

1.7.4 A proposal for the establishment of a Me dical College on PPP basis is also under the

college on PPP model for Andaman and Nicobar Islands, may be taken expeditiously.

DEMAND No. 97-DAMAN AND DIU 
1.12 GOALS/TARGETS 
Recommendation 
1.12.1  The Committee recommends that a holistic Vision Statement regarding overall development of 
the UT be prepared comprising of realistic goals achievable within a given time frame and 
quantifiable benchmarks prescribed so that progress made in the Plan period could be measured and 
the development policies/schemes adjusted according to the performance on the ground. (Para 5.13.2 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.12.2  UT Administration of Daman and Diu has decided to accept the overall vision of Planning 
Commission for 11th Five Year Plan Period with specific attention on Health, Education, Water 
Supply, Energy, Transport, Touris m, Urban Development and Industry. UT Administration has also 
prepared the Annual Action Plan specifying quantifiable targets to be achieved during 2010-11 by all 
the Departments and the progress made/performance of all the Departments shall be measured in 
terms of the targets/benchmarks achieved in implementing all the Plan Schemes/Centrally Sponsored 
Schemes, etc. vis-a-vis the targets/benchmarks set in the Annual Action Plan. This exercise shall be 
repeated in future years as well. 
1.12.3  The Sector specific vision is as under: 
1.  QUALITY HEALTH FOR ALL 
1.12.4  One of the targets fixed for 11th Plan under Health Sector is reduction of Infant Mortality 
Rate (IMR) to 28 against present rate of 60 for India. In the U. T. of Daman and Diu. IMR for the 
calendar year 2009 was 31/1000 live birth. However, the aim of UT Administration will be to improve 
quality of health services particularly in rural areas during 11th Plan period. In order to bring and 
improve all health facilities in Rural areas under one umbrella, a Centrally Sponsored Scheme, 
National Rural Health Mission is being implemented in the U.T. of Daman and. Diu. Major Schemes 
proposed for 11th Plan under this sector are establishment of Oncology Centre at Daman, setting up of 
three additional PHCs in Daman and one additional PHC in Diu, increase in bed capacity, upgradation 
of Primary Health Centres to Community Health Cent res, establishment of one Mental Health Unit at 
CHC, Ghoghla, Diu and Statistical Cell/Health Information Cell in all the institutions. 
2.  100% LITERACY AND DEVELOPMENT OF SKILL 
1.12.5  Education is the most critical input for empowering people with skills, knowledge and access 
to employment in future. Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan is being 
implemented in U.T. of Daman and Diu also which aims at free elementary education to all children in 
the age group of 6-14 years by 2010. This is necessa ry to achieve literacy rate of 80% proposed after 
end of Eleventh Five Year Plan. The literacy rate has increased from 71 % in 1991 to 78% in 2001 in 
U.T. of Daman & Diu. The literacy ra te in this U.T. is much higher than the Literacy Rate of India, 
which is 64% in 2001. Literacy Rate is comparativel y lower for weaker sections of the society such as 
SC, ST and Women for whom various schemes for providing educational incentives such as 

Textbooks, Stationery, Uniform and Scholarship, are being implemented. Gender gap in literacy is 
proposed to be reduced to 10% by the end of Eleventh Plan. 
1.12.6  There is one Government College (for Graduation), Six Higher Secondary Schools, 21 
Secondary Schools, 23 Middle Schools, 51 Primar y Schools and 19 Pre-Primary Schools including 
private schools. Besides, two Ashramshalas for tribal boys and one Navodaya Vidyalaya are 
functioning in Daman. For Technical Education, there is one Polytechnic College and one B.Ed. 
College in Daman. One Technical Training Institute and one Industrial Training Institute is in each 
District. 
1.12.7  Elementary Education has been entrusted to District Panchayat which need major amount for 
construction of additional classrooms and toilet facilities for primary and middle schools. Under 
Secondary Education, some Middle Schools are proposed to be upgraded as Secondary School and 
some Secondary Schools are proposed to be upgraded as Higher Secondary School. During the 
Eleventh Plan, it is proposed to establish one Government College and one Kendriya Vidyalaya at 
Diu. The grants given to Local Bodies and the incentives given to Scheduled Castes students like 
Scholarship, Uniform, Books etc. are also proposed to be substantially enhanced during the Eleventh 
Plan. 
3.  SAFE DRINKING WATER FOR ALL 
1.12.8  Safe drinking water has been considered as the most important and basic requirement for all 
population. Under this Sector, schemes for procurement of raw water from Sardar Sarovar Dam of 
Gujarat for Diu District, establishment of Reverse Osmosis Plant at Diu District and creation of 
infrastructure facilities for water supply in rural and urban areas of Daman and Diu Districts have 
been proposed. 
1.12.9  It has also been planned to provide safe drinking water to Daman District through pipeline 
from Madhuben Dam thereby avoiding chemical contamination of water which is being carried 
through open canal at present. 
1.12.10  Similarly, it has been planned to procure Raw Water from Sardar Sarovar Canal of Gujarat 
State for Diu. The water will be supplied through pipeline from Una, Gujarat to Diu. 
4.  PROVIDING UNINTERRUPTED AND RELIABLE POWER SUPPLY 
1.12.11  Rapid Industrial growth has led to tremendous increase in electric power demand. In the U.T. 
of Daman and Diu, all villages have been electrified. The U.T. of Daman & Diu does not have its own 
power generation. Power supply is drawn from Central sector power stations and the same is 
transmitted and distributed by Electricity Department in Daman & Diu through one Sub Station at 
Daman of 220/66 K.V. and seven Sub Stations of 66/11 K.V. ( six in Daman and one in Diu). Total 
capacity of all Sub Stations is 332 M.V.A. against peak demand of 240 M.V.A. Annual requirement of 
power is around 1600 M.U. costing Rs. 490 crore approximately. 
1.12.12  In order to provide uninterrupted and reliable power supply, overhead lines are being 
converted into under ground lines in phased manner which will be completed by the end of Eleventh 
Five Year Plan. Capacity of various Sub- Stations has been proposed to be enhanced during Eleventh 
Five Year Plan. 

1.12.13  In order to meet the increasing need of power supply by industries of Dabhel and Kachigam, 
a new Sub Station of 220/60 K.V. with capacity of 100 MY A has been proposed to be installed at 
Ringanwada Village of Daman District during Eleventh Plan. One Sub Station of 66/11 KV with 
capacity of 30 MVA has also been proposed at Bhimpore Village of Daman District. 
5.  QUALITY ROADS UP TO THE DOOR STEPS OF EVERY HOUSE 
1.12.14  It is necessary to improve mobility and easy  accessibility in order to achieve desired level of 
growth in development. Transport sector is key for development in all economic activities. As a part 
of modernization of the Transport Department, the Pilot Project of VAHAN Software has been 
implemented for maintaining the registration records of the vehicles during the Eleventh Five Year 
Plan in Daman District. 
1.12.15  In U.T. of Daman and Diu, all villages are connected by all weather motorable roads. Rural 
roads are being constructed and repaired by District Panchayat under Centrally Sponsored Scheme of 
Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY). Besides roads, Bridges are very important for 
development activities in this V.T. In Daman District, construction of a new bridge over Damanganga 
river joining Moti Daman and Nani Daman has been completed during the Financial Year 2008-09. In 
addition, following new bridges have been proposed to be constructed during Eleventh Plan. 
(i) High level bridges at Zari Causeway and Pataliya Causeway in Daman District. 
(ii) Bridge at Diu connecting Va nakbara (Diu) to Kotda (Gujarat) 
(iii) Completion of Tud Bridge connecting Diu to Una (Gujarat) 
(v) Major roads in Daman District are being converted into four lanes. 
1.12.16  UT Administration has taken up construction of new four-lane bye-pass road (i.e. Coastal 
Highway) from Patalia to Bhenslore at Nani Daman for a length of 5.500 Kms. During the Financial 
Year 2009-10 and the same will be completed during the current Financial Year 2010-11. 
6.  TOURISM WITH ADVENTURE AND PEACE 
1.I2.I 7  Tourism sector has great potential for rapid growth in economy. In U.T. of Daman and Diu, 
there is good scope for tourism development. Daman and Diu both have natural and historical tourist 
spots like beaches, forts, churches, temples etc. Tourists come here not only from India but also from 
foreign countries. Nearly 10 lakh tourists visit Daman and Diu annually. Hence, new projects have 
been proposed under tourism for providing Ropeway from Gangeshwar at Fudam to Pothiadada 
Temple at Kevdi. Construction of Modern type fish aquarium, construction of Ultra Fast Action 
Musical Fountain at Diu, purchase of 60 Seater new Luxury tourist boat and development of gardens, 
beaches, tourist spots, water sports activities have been proposed in Daman and Diu. 
7.  URBAN DEVELOPMENT SCHEMES 
1.12.18  Urbanisation is increasing rapidly all over India. Daman and Diu have the oldest history of 
urbanization as these Districts have oldest Municipalities in Asia formed during 15th Century under 
Portuguese rule. In order to provide necessary infrastructure and improve civic amenities, a Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme of Urban Infrastructure Development of Small and Medium Towns (UIDSSMT) is 
being implemented in selected cities and towns including Daman & Diu. The underground sewerage 

project has been proposed under this scheme in Moti Daman. The said project is going to be 
implemented in 2010-11 if approved by the Ministry of Urban Development, Government of India. 
UT Administration proposes to substantially increase the Grant-in- Aid to Municipal Councils of 
Daman & Diu so that they can execute important Urba n development projects such as construction of 
slaughter house, construction of Fish Market, Vegetable Market, construction of Municipal Council’s 
office building, construction of Community Hall, construction, repair and maintenance of Urban 
roads, construction of Sea Protection wall, providi ng drainage facilities, cleanliness of Urban area, 
maintenance of Parks etc. 
8.  GROWTH WITH HEALTHY ENVIRONMENT 
1.12.19  Industries contribute to National Income as well as provide employment to local people. 
Industry Sector has gained good strength over past  fifteen years as a consequence of liberalizing 
industrial policies for integration with world economy. 
1.12.20  In order to provide better infrastructure facilities for Industries such as Roads, Street Lights, 
drainage system and raw materials, higher outlay has been proposed by UT Administration under 
Industry Sector during Eleventh Plan. To display/ex hibit different industrial products of Daman and 
Diu Districts, UT Administration propose to participate in National and Inter - National Trade 
Industrial Fairs during the Eleventh Plan. It also proposes to enhance the equity share in the Omnibus 
Industrial Development Corporation, Daman during the Eleventh Plan, and also to generate additional 
revenue for the Government.

after April 2009 till 23rd April 2010 was thus better.

however start from 2012 and later years. 
1.14.8  UT Administration has requested the Ministry of Power, Government of India, vide  letter 
dated, 24.04.2010 for relooking into the revision of the power allocation to reduce the gap between 
supply and demand.

rate of Rs.2.84 per unit which is much less in comparison to the rates of Rs.5.00 to Rs.5.50 per unit in

supra
.
