3.1 ROLE OF CIVIL DEFENCE IN CHANGING SCENARIO
Recommendation
3.1.1 The role of Civil Defence should be seen in the light of the paradigm shift in the security
scenario of the country and that it should be in consonance with the changing times. Modern civil
defence cannot be effective unless it gears to the new challenges of proxy war, terrorism, communal
riots and other civic strife which cause loss of life and property. Since traditional warfare is no
longer a major component of threat, the new security climate requires prompt response to new threat
instruments like proxy war, terrorism, acts of sabotage and subversion.
(Para 14.1.1 of 136
th Report )
Action Taken
3.1.2 Civil Defence in India operates under the statutory authority of the Civil Defence Act, 1968
and is intended to be organized primarily on a voluntary basis as an integral part of the defence
of the country on a limited scale. Civil Defence being a community based organization presents a
unique opportunity for community policing and they have acquired certain skills in crisis prevention
and recovery.
3.1.3 A Centrally Sponsored Scheme for Revamping Civil Defence set up in the country at an
estimated cost of Rs.100 crore for implementation in the Eleventh Plan Period has been approved
and sanctioned by the Government of India. The Scheme inter alia, include upgradation of existing
State Training Institutes in terms of infrastructure, transport and equipment, construction of 10
new State Training Institutes, upgradation of facilities in 100 identified Civil Defence towns. The
Scheme envisages converting the Civil Defence from town-centric to district-centric. As a part of
this scheme, a pilot project at a cost of Rs.3.25 crore is being undertaken to involve Civil Defence
volunteers in assisting the Police in law and order and internal security situations. The overall
objective of the pilot project is to interpret the law more liberally to include internal security threats
like terrorist and extremist violence, communal violence among the reasons for involving Civil
Defence measures. This pilot project envisages 10 days’ intensive training for 214 hand-picked Civil
Defence Wardens/ V olunteers from 17 Major and 23 Minor towns from different States at National
Civil Defence College (NCDC), Nagpur in batches.
3.1.4 After the completion of training at NCDC, Nagpur, these Master Trainers, with the help of
guest faculties, will impart training to trainers in their respective State Training Institutes to 4280
volunteers/wardens (1000 from Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai, Bangalore and Hyderabad, 1440 from other
12 major towns and 1840 from 23 Minor Towns).
3.1.5 Trainers trained in the State Training Institutes will be involved in various types of
orientation programmes, drills, etc. to be organized in coordination with the police authorities and
will also assist them in orientation programmes which will include seminars, workshops, rallies,
demonstrations, and exercises. Through these programmes, all the Civil Defence volunteers residing

11
in the jurisdiction of local police stations will be given orientation by the trained Master Trainers
and trained Civil Defence volunteers in intelligence gathering, surveillance, maintenance of
communal harmony, national integration, precautions in case of bomb scare and protective
measures before the bomb is detected/defused, tenant verification, general vigilance with reference
to possible terrorist activities, various response activities including evacuation of casualties, first aid
and establishment of relief camps etc. All these activities will be conducted under the overall
supervision of Controller/Deputy Controller of Civil Defence in consultation with local police
authorities. Detailed guidelines as to how these activities have to be carried out, role of civil
authorities and the coordination mechanism with police authorities and Civil Defence volunteers/
wardens has been issued separately by Director General (NCRF & CD).
3.1.6 So far, 185 Master Trainers have already completed their training at NCDC, Nagpur, and
the training of trainers at State level has commenced in some of the States. The remaining 29
trainees will be trained in the course commencing on 08.02.2010. Thereafter the training of trainers
will commence in all the States, where pilot project has been launched. Their work will be
reviewed for gauging their operational and administrative efficiency by the end of calendar year
2010. Based on the impact assessment of the project, its replication in other districts/towns could
be considered. The project is being closely monitored by the Director General (NCRF & CD) as
well as MHA on regular basis.
3.1.7 Further issues raised
• The status of pilot projects of Civil Defence in 100 selected towns.
• Whether operational and administrative efficiency review proposed to be undertaken by
the end of 2010, has been undertaken; if so, the details thereof?
• Composition of professional services, which have been entrusted to manage working of
Civil Defence institutions.
3.1.8 Response of the Government
(i) Status of Pilot Project:-  Under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for Revamping of Civil
Defence Setup in the Country a Pilot Project has been launched in 40 Selected towns to
involve Civil Defence V olunteers in Internal Security duties. As against a target of Training
214 Masters Trainers all 214 have been trained and against a target of training of 4,280
Civil Defence V olunteers by these master trainers at State level 3,267 volunteers have
already been trained. These volunteers are now to be deployed by the States for Community
policing and intelligence gathering.
(ii) The scheme was sanctioned in 2009. Initially, the funds were allocated to States as grant-
in-aid for various activities of the scheme. The actual work on ground started in the
Financial Year 2010-11. Hence, a mid-term review of the scheme, “Revamping of Civil
Defence set up in the country” is now planned in 2011-12.
(iii) No professional services have been earmarked in the scheme to manage working of Civil
Defence institutions in the States as it is the responsibility of the State Governments to
provide manpower for the Civil Defence institutes. Large number of vacancies exists in the
permanent Civil Defence staff at CD headquarters’ and state level C.D training institutes
which need to be filled up by the State Governments.
Further Recommendation
3.1.9 The Committee is constrained to note that as against a target of training of 4,280

12
Civil Defence Volunteers by these master trainers at State level, only 3,267 volunteers have
been trained. Since the civil defence apparatus has mainly volunteers at the lower level, the
top implementing leadership should be professional so that it can guide volunteers well.
3.1.10 The Committee takes a serious view of the fact that there are a large number of
vacancies in the permanent Civil Defence staff at CD headquarters’ and state level CD
training institutes. In this scenario, the Civil Defence set up cannot function efficiently. The
Committee strongly recommends that early steps may be taken to fill up the vacancies.
3.2 ADEQUATE TRAINING AND PROFESSIONALISATION OF CIVIL DEFENCE
APPARATUS
Recommendation
3.2.1 The Committee is of the view that Civil Defence should be made more professional as the
challenges have grown extremely complex and require a more sophisticated response. This, in turn,
requires better training and higher professionalism. The Committee is also of the view that a sense
of professionalism is essential to be infused among the ranks of Civil Defence organization across
the country in order to augment its capability to deal with the potential challenges which are
growingly assuming complex characteristics warranting sophisticated response for safety of lives
and properties. The sophistication can be achieved by encouraging professionalism in the civil
defence organization and by imparting better training.
(Para 15.1 of 136
th Report )
Action Taken
3.2.2 A Centrally Sponsored Scheme for Revamping of Civil Defence has been approved for
implementation during the Eleventh Plan period at an estimated cost of Rs.100 crore. The Scheme
lays emphasis on enhancing the capabilities of the existing Civil Defence organization by
upgradation of existing 17 State Training Institutes (STIs), creation of 10 new STIs, grant of
equipments and transport required for training. Proposals have been received from 12 States for
strengthening of existing institutes. Out of the Rs.15 crore sanctioned for revamping of Civil
Defence during the current year, an amount of Rs.14.55 crore has been released to the concerned
State Government by the DG (NDRF&CD). DG, NDRF & CD has been regularly monitoring the
progress of the scheme.
3.2.3 National Civil Defence College at Nagpur is also being strengthened/upgraded in terms of
building, infrastructure, transport and equipment for capacity building of Civil Defence personnel
and volunteers.
3.2.4 To encourage professionalism among the volunteers, the existing register of Civil Defence
Corps is being revised on regular basis by Director General of Civil Defence to weed out incapable,
infirm and weak volunteers. So far 21,628 Civil Defence volunteers have been weeded out from
the register of the Civil Defence and 20,370 new volunteers have been enrolled.
3.2.5 Public awareness campaign will be undertaken as a part of the Scheme to motivate people
of good social standing to join Civil Defence. Efforts will be made to inculcate a sense of
professionalism among the wardens/volunteers.
3.2.6 Further issues raised
• 20,370 new volunteers have been enrolled against 21,628  weeded out. In this
background, how the shortfall is made up and at what intervals this exercise of
weeding out is done?

13
• Whether Government has any plan to rope in, subject to fitness, retired public servants
as civil defence volunteers?
3.2.7 Response of the Government
The weeding out exercise was carried out as a onetime measure where all enrolled Civil
Defence volunteers were screened for efficiency, age and physical fitness. A total of 62,904
volunteers were weeded out after Jan 2009 and 54,389 new volunteers were enrolled. Thereafter
the weeding out is to be carried out periodically and vacancies filled by new volunteers by the
States. There is no maximum age limit for joining Civil Defence organization and as such retired
public servants are eligible to join civil defence organization subject to their physical fitness and
mental fitness.
Further Recommendations
3.2.8 The Committee notes that a total of 62,904 volunteers were weeded out after
January 2009 and 54,389 new volunteers were enrolled, thus leaving a substantial shortfall
in the strength of total number of volunteers. The Committee is of the considered view
that concrete steps are required to be taken to fill the shortfall, if Civil Defence system
is to be strengthened and for its proper functioning. Public awareness campaigns are
needed to be undertaken on a regular intervals. A plan may be chalked out to infuse
professionalism.
3.3 NEED FOR BROAD BASING CIVIL DEFENCE
Recommendation
3.3.1 The Committee is of the view that the present classification of Civil Defence towns in
various categories is irrelevant in today’ s context as the modern missile technology has brought
virtually every inch of the country’s territory in its target. A more realistic classification according
to the present security and strategic environment should be drawn up with a view to ensure that
trained Civil Defence volunteer forces are raised in every possible nook and corners of the country
who can be called for duty to the society envisaged inter -alia under Article 51A (i) of the
Constitution of India.
(Para 17.1 of 136
th Report )
Action taken
3.3.2 The core recommendation of the Shri K.M. Singh’s Committee report is that the Civil
Defence set up presently limited to towns should be made district-centric and should cover all the
600+ districts. The Second Administrative Reforms Commission in its Third Report on Crisis
Management has recommended that efforts should be made to enroll 1% of the total population of
the country under Civil Defence. This can be achieved by spreading the Civil Defence to all
districts of the country in a phased manner.
3.3.3 Based on above recommendations, Rs.4.00 crore has been allocated to reorient the town-
specific Civil Defence set up into a district-wise entity in 100 identified multi-hazard prone
districts within in the Scheme of Revamping Civil Defence setup being implemented during the
current Plan Period. In 36 districts out of the 100 identified multi-hazard prone districts, Civil
Defence setup does not exist and will be raised under the present Scheme. Eventually, all the 600
districts of the country will be covered in phases so that Civil Defence organization spread
throughout the country.

14
3.3.4 Further issues raised
• Civil Defence setup does not exist in 36 districts out of the 100 districts identified for
multihazard prone districts. What steps have been taken to raise Civil Defence
infrastructure in these districts?
• Whether any blue print to cover all the 600 districts has been prepared; if so, the
details thereof; and if not, by when the same will be ready?
3.3.5 Response of the Government
A total of 100 districts have been identified as multi hazard Civil Defence (CD) districts,
out of which 36 districts not considered as CD districts earlier have now been notified as CD
districts and State Governments have been authorized to raise CD organization there. Based on the
feedback received from these 100 CD districts, a plan to cover all the 600 districts as CD districts
in phases is to be prepared for uniform spread of CD organization.
Further Recommendation
3.3.6 The Committee is dismayed to note that in the 36 districts, out of the 100 districts
identified for multi-hazard prone districts, Civil Defence setup does not exist. The
Committee strongly recommends that steps be taken to raise civil defence infrastructure in
these districts as soon as possible. The Committee hopes that after the successful
completion of the first phase, and based on the feedback received from the 100 CD districts,
the plan to cover all the 600 districts in the country as CD districts in phases may be
prepared and implemented soon.
3.4 INTEGRATING CIVIL DEFENCE ORGANIZATION WITH NCC/NSS AND NYKS
Recommendation
3.4.1 The Committee is of the view that a workable linkage between the various youth
organizations and Civil Defence for the purpose of strengthening the Disaster Management effort
can be developed by synergizing all efforts and resources of the various agencies involved and
capacity-building measures for developing trained human resource.
(Para 21.1 of 136
th Report )
3.4.2 Youth organizations such as National Cadet Corps (NCC), Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangthan
(NYKS), and National Service Scheme (NSS), which invariably comprise of volunteers belonging to
Schools, Colleges and Universities, although have the inherent advantage of reaching out to the
grass-roots level and their ready availability for immediate assistance in the event of any disaster
and have been rightly recommended by the High Power Committee for focusing emphasis on greater
coordination with these youth organization, the Committee find the shortcoming in the said
recommendation of the High Power Committee conspicuous in restricting the endeavour only within
the youth who have the privilege of receiving formal education in schools, colleges and universities
and, thus, leaving a vast pool of un-educated youth, whose number must be substantial in the
country where approximately 43  per cent people are illiterate, outside the Civil Defence endeavour
because they can neither be members of NCC nor NYKS nor NSS. The Committee, therefore, urges
upon the Ministry of Home Affairs to make sincere efforts in seeking the cooperation and
coordination of various youth organizations as well as to ensure involvement as Volunteers also of
non-student youths right from the village panchayat level upto the level of each Civil Defence
district.
(Para 21.2 of 136
th Report )

15
Action Taken
3.4.3 Ministries of Defence and Youth Affairs have been approached to seek cooperation for
motivating the members of various youth organization such as NCC, NYKS and NSS etc. to join
the Civil Defence Corps as volunteers. In order to achieve the objective of enhanced capacity
building, they have been requested to issue appropriate instructions to chief co-coordinators and
office bearers of these organizations at State/ district levels to co-operate and co-ordinate with
controllers of Civil Defence for active interaction and extending cooperation in organizing activities
to train and motivate youths of these organization to become Civil Defence volunteers. Director
General of Civil Defence has also requested Civil Defence authority in the State to seek their
cooperation and to achieve better coordination between the Civil Defence authorities and office
bearers of various Youth Organizations at State/ district level for enrolling the members of these
organizations as Civil Defence volunteers. As per report received from the States, Civil Defence
training is being imparted in schools and colleges. NCC Cadets of Schools and Colleges are also
motivated and imparted training and are potential Civil Defence V olunteers after they finish their
studies.
3.4.4 Once the existing approach of towns centric gets re-oriented to district centric, the youth
at village/block level will also be encouraged to join Civil Defence set up through motivation and
awareness generation programmes. The cadres of NSS & NYKS will also be roped in to take active
part in Civil Defence activities.
3.4.5 Further issues raised
• Steps taken to integrate youth outside the formal organization in Civil Defence so as
to tap the vast human resource of less educated youths;
• The legal institutional framework made so far and motivational schemes floated for
attracting the youth for the purpose.
• Whether any centralized data having profile of volunteers viz. age group, profession
and other necessary items, is being maintained; if so, details thereof and how many
enrolled volunteers are from NCC, NKYS and NSS.
3.4.6 Response of the Government
(i) In  order to attract the desirable quality of youth to join as Civil Defence volunteers an
amount of Rs.3 crores has been provisioned in the Scheme for carrying out publicity at
both Central and State level. In  addition Rs.5.5 crores has been provisioned to conduct
training camps/exercises and demonstrations for Civil Defence volunteers in States/UTs. In
order to attract the youth, no legal-institutional framework for tapping less educated youth
exists as of now since “the basic educational qualification to become a Civil Defence
volunteer is only primary standard and this also can be relaxed on the discretion of
controller civil defence in the district” as laid down in Civil Defence Regulations.
(ii) As the Civil Defence is a State subject, the CD setup in States is managed and maintained
entirely by the State Governments. The Central Government does not maintain any
centralized data of civil defence volunteers on regular basis as all volunteers are enrolled,
trained equipped and paid by the State Governments. Data on civil defence is obtained from
States on as required basis.

16
Further recommendations
3.4.7 The Committee is of the view that the vast population of less educated youth still
remains untapped. The services of such vast resource in far flung areas should not be
ignored. A proper institutional mechanism can efficiently tap this huge potential. The
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that Government should not only make legal
framework and institutional arrangement for the purpose, but motivational schemes may
also prepared and implemented for attracting the educated as well as the less educated
youth.

17
CHAPTER-IV
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF
WHICH THE FINAL REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT
HAVE NOT YET BEEN RECEIVED BY THE COMMITTEE
4.1 PUBLIC-PRIV ATE PARTNERSHIP IN CIVIL DEFENCE
Recommendation
4.1.1 The Committee recommends that private sector having good track record should be
encouraged to participate in civil defence activities through tax exemptions on contributions made
in such activities. They can also be persuaded to sponsor seminars and other awareness programmes
as part of their social responsibility. The Committee recommends that private sector entities,
including enterprising individual citizens, should be encouraged to participate in building and
maintaining civil defence activities inter alia by way of granting exemption from Tax to financial
contributions made towards such activities, including sponsoring of seminars and other public
awareness programmes etc. as part of their social responsibility.
(Para 16.1 of 136
th Report )
Action taken
4.1.2 The recommendation of Shri K.M. Singh Committee for enhancing public-private-partnership
through voluntary contribution by private corporate sector to the Civil Defence setup was endorsed
by the Home Minister’s Civil Defence Advisory Committee during its meeting held in April, 2008
at New Delhi.
4.1.3 Proposal for considering tax exemption to the private sector for contribution/donation to
Civil Defence organization has been forwarded to Department of Revenue on 19.2.2009.
Department of Revenue is being pursued to take a decision.
4.1.4 Further issues raised
• What is the response of the Department of Revenue on the issue of providing tax
exemptions to the private sector for contribution/donation to Civil Defence
organization?
• What are the other proposals to attract the private sector to Civil Defence?
• Whether the matter of extending-tax exemption was again pursued with the Department
of Revenue before finalization of the Budget 2011-12; if so, the response thereof?
4.1.5 Response of the Government
A reference was made to Department of Revenue on 19.2.2009 for tax-exemption under
Income-Tax Act on donation/contributions given by the private/corporate sector to Civil Defence
activities. However neither response was received from Department of Revenue nor has any
notification regarding tax exemption been received. No reference has been made to the Department
of Revenue for tax exemption before finalization of the Budget 2011-12.
17

18
Further recommendation
4.1.6 The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs may follow up with
Department of Revenue for tax-exemption under Income-Tax Act on donation/contributions
given by the private/corporate sector to Civil Defence activities and the response of the
Department of Revenue may be informed to this Committee.

The Committee recommends that the Government should make all out efforts to

The Committee is constrained to note that as against a target of training of 4,280

(Para 3.1.9)

(Para 3.2.8)

The Committee is dismayed to note that in the 36 districts, out of the 100 districts

Committee strongly recommends that steps be taken to raise civil defence infrastructure in

The Committee is of the view that the vast population of less educated youth still

Affairs, having been authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred and Fifty Third Report on the Action Taken by Government on the
recommendations/observations contained in its One Hundred and Thirty Fifth Report on Border
Fencing and Floodlighting Projects along Indo-Pak Border pertaining to the Ministry of Home
Affairs.

Committee on Home Affairs was presented to the Parliament on 21
th October, 2008.

Notes on One Hundred and Thirty Fifth Report on Border Fencing and Floodlighting Projects along
Indo-Pak Border. The present Action Taken Report of the Committee has been prepared on the
basis of the updated Action Taken Notes.

27
th July, 2011.

Home Affairs on the recommendations contained in the One Hundred and Thirty Fifth Report of
the Committee on border fencing and floodlighting projects along the Indo-Pak border. The One
Hundred Thirty Fifth Report was presented to/laid on the Table of Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha on
the 21
st October, 2008.

CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH
HA VE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
1.1 EXPEDITIOUS APPROVAL OF REVISED COST
Recommendation
1.1.1 The Committee understands that the geographical and topographical location of the region
as well as remoteness and tough terrain conditions of Rann have greatly hampered the border
fencing and floodlighting projects. The financial anticipated revised cost to the tune of Rs.1210
crore was under the consideration of Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS). The Committee
recommends that the revised cost may be expeditiously approved by CCS for early completion of
the works.
(Para 2.5.1 )
Action Taken
1.1.2 Approval of the Cabinet Committee on Security for revised cost of Rs.1201 crore has been
obtained on 20th July 2009. The works of construction of fencing, road, floodlighting and Border
Out Posts has since resumed in Gujarat Sector and the entire works are targeted to be completed
by 2011-12 or three working seasons whichever is later.
Further Recommendation
1.1.3 The Committee desires that the construction work of fencing, road, floodlighting and
Border Outposts in Gujarat Sector may be completed as per schedule.
1.2 COMPLETION OF THE CONSTRUCTION OF BORDER ROADS WITHOUT FURTHER
DELAY
Recommendation
1.2.1 The Committee is constrained to observe that the work of construction of border roads has
not been taken up seriously. Out of total length of 134  kms. which was required to be constructed.
73.5 kms. road has been allotted to CPWD and 60.5 kms. to the NBCC. Out of 73.5  kms., CPWD
has constructed only 49 kms. road. NBCC too has not completed its work. The Committee strongly
recommends that Government must make an inquiry into the matter and direct the agencies
concerned to complete the construction of border roads without further delay, for effective
patrolling of the border areas by BSF personnel.
(Para 2.5.3 )
Action Taken
1.2.3 Out of 340 km. border roads sanctioned in Gujarat sector construction work of 260 km.
stretch has been completed and work on 20 km. is now in progress. Construction of the balance
pending works has been approved by the Competent Authority and financial releases have been
made. The executing agencies, viz., Central Public Works Department (CPWD) and National

3
Building Construction Corporation (NBCC) have been directed to expedite the progress and
complete the remaining works in the schedule manner.
Further Recommendation
1.2.4 The Committee recommends that the work in progress may be completed at the
earliest. The balance pending works may be taken up and completed as per targets without
time and cost overruns.
1.3 REALIGNING THE FENCE TOWARDS THE ZERO LINE
Recommendation
1.3.1 It has been brought to the notice of the Committee that the Indian farmers sow the crops
in the large land located between the fencing line and international border areas which is very
fertile. Unfortunately, during the harvest time the crops are taken away by the people from the
other side of the border with the connivance and support of the border guarding forces of the
neighbouring country. The Committee is of the view that the problem being faced by our farmers
is expected to be minimized with the forward shifted of this stretch of fence.
(Para 3.6.2 )
Action Taken
1.3.2 Realignment of the fence towards the zero line, due to large tracks of cultivable land lying
ahead of the present fencing alignment, has been considered by the Government. A proposal for
forward shifting of 23.380 km. of fencing closer to zero line in Ferozpur sector has been approved
by Government in January 2008 and work is in progress.
Further Recommendation
1.3.3 The Committee recommends that there should not be any delay in the completion of
the project on shifting of 23,380 kms. of fencing closur e to Zero Line in Ferozpur Sector. The
Committee desires to be informed of the time frame by when the work will be completed.
1.4 WOMEN CONSTABLES TO BE DEPLOYED AT THE FENCING GATES FOR FRISKING
OF WOMEN FARMERS
Recommendation
1.4.1 The Committee further recommends that the recruitment of 685  women constables to be
deployed at the fencing gates for frisking of women farmers, should be completed at the earliest
so that no inconvenience is caused to the women farmers while being frisked.
(Para 3.6.3 )
Action Taken
1.4.2 Government has sanctioned 745 posts of women constables in BSF out of which 658 have
been deployed at the fencing gates for frisking of women farmers and 87 are undergoing training.
1.5 CHANGE IN COMPOSITION OF METAL USED IN THE FENCE
Recommendation
1.5.1 The Committee has been officially informed that painting of fence is being done regularly

4
as per specifications and budget and for this purpose funds have been allocated to the battalions.
However, the Committee has been given to understand that there are some funds constraints in this
regard. Considering the condition of weather in the area and to avoid recurring cost, the Committee
recommends that the composition of metal used in the fence should be changed and fencing may
be done by using good quality galvanized iron or steel.
(Para 3.6.4 )
Action Taken
1.5.2 The construction agencies entrusted with fencing work have been directed to maintain the
quality of fencing and take remedial measures. They have also been advised to use good quality
galvonised iron or steel in fencing in consideration of hostile weather condition in border areas.
1.6 ONE MORE BATTALION AT THE FEROZPUR SECTOR
Recommendation
1.6.1 The Committee desires that the issue of raising one more battalion at the Ferozpur Sector,
may be examined in the Ministry of Home Affairs as this is a hyper sensitive area.
(Para 3.10.2 )
Action Taken by the Government
1.6.2  As per the requirement projected by BSF, the MHA has recently considered augmentation
of manpower of BSF and has accorded sanction to raise additional 29 Battalions, 7 Sector
Headquarters and 3 Frontier Headquarters in 5 phases from the financial year 2009-10 to 2013-14.
Key location plans have also been approved.
Further Recommendation
1.6.3 The Committee desires that Ferozpur Sector may be included among the key
locations plans.
1.7 CHALLENGES IN PROPER MANAGEMENT OF THE BORDER
Recommendation
1.7.1 It is the understanding of the Committee that proper management of the Border spells out
many challenges viz. coordination and concerted action by administrative, diplomatic, security,
intelligence, legal, regulatory and financial agencies of the country to secure the frontiers and
subserve its interests. Keeping in view these facts, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of
Home Affairs should chalk out a strategic Action Plan which may include construction of effective
and quality fencing, floodlighting and concrete roads along the border areas; deployment of high
tech surveillance equipments on the border; strengthening of security of coastal borders of the
country etc.
(Para 3.11.2 )
Action Taken by the Government
1.7.2 The Government has accorded high priority to the construction of fencing, border roads
and floodlighting along Indo-Bangladesh and Indo-Pakistan border. Out of 3436 km. of fencing and
4326 km. of border roads sanctioned by the Government, 2677 km. of fencing and 3330 km. of
border roads have been completed along Indo-Bangladesh border. Remaining works are expected to

5
be completed by March, 2012. Besides, 277 km. of floodlighting has also been completed along
Indo-Bangladesh border and a project for construction of 2840 km. of floodlighting is currently
under progress.
1.7.3 Along Indo-Pakistan border, 1948 km. of fencing and 1861 km. of floodlighting has been
completed out of sanctioned length of 2043 km. and 2009 km. respectively. Balance works in
Gujarat sector are under progress.
1.7.4 To redress the inadequacy of infrastructure along Indo-China Border, the Government has
undertaken the construction of 27 strategic roads totaling 804 km. length. The work of
construction in respect of 21 roads has since started and the entire project is targeted to be
completed by March 2013.
1.7.5 In order to strengthen the coastal security, a supplemental scheme is under implementation
in 9 coastal States and 4 Union Territories. Under this scheme, 71 Coastal Police Stations have been
set up out of 73 sanctioned by the Government. Interceptor boats to the Coastal States and Union
Territories are also being provided for effective surveillance of the coastal borders. The coastal
security Phase-II scheme has also been approved by the Government for implementation w.e.f.
April 2011.
1.7.6 Apart from the above measures, Border Guarding Forces have been/are being equipped with
hi-tech surveillance equipments like Hand Held Thermal Imagers, Long Range Reconnaissance
Observation System, Mobile Surveillance V ehicles, Binoculars, etc., which are acting as force
multiplier for effective border management.
1.7.7 The measures enumerated above will go a long way in effective management of the borders
of the country.

2.1 WATER SUPPLY FOR THE BSF PERSONNEL
Recommendation
2.1.1 The Committee notes that the place of worship in the border areas are closely intertwined
with daily life of ESF Jawans. It is of the considered view of the Committee that if water tank/
reservoirs/lakes could be constructed near such places of worship, it would to a great extend solve
the daily necessity of the Jawans as well as the cattle of the farmers. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs should come out with suitable scheme for providing
water tanks/reservoir/lakes near the places of worship located near the frontier areas.
(Para 2.3.5 )
Action Taken
2.1.2 The Government has introduced several schemes for providing drinking and potable water
to the border districts under Border Area Development Programme. BSF has however, been asked
to prepare a consolidated proposal for construction of water tanks/reservoirs/lakes, etc. near the
places of worship in border areas in consultation with their field formations. MHA proposes to
provide funds for this purpose under the Border Area Development Programme.

THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT

3.1 STELLAR ROLE OF BSF IN GUARDING THE COUNTRY’S FRONTIERS
Recommendation
3.1.1 The Committee hails the stellar role of BSF in guarding the country’ s frontiers under
tremendous adverse circumstances due to geographical, climatic and other conditions. Our borders
are secure due to their diligence, loyalty and commitment to their arduous duty. The Committee duly
acknowledges their patriotism. In this context, the Committee strongly recommends that the
Government should provide better conditions of living and better conditions of service to BSF
personnel. The Committee also recommends to the Government to grant desert/remote areas
allowance and ration money. The Government should also expedite the opening of Kendriya
Vidyalaya in the border areas so that the education of the children of the BSF jawans is not
neglected on account of posting in frontier areas.
(Para 2.3.1 )
Action Taken
3.1.2 The Government is committed to provide better living and service conditions to the BSF
personnel. In pursuance of this objective, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has granted
accommodation allowance, consequent upon the implementation of the 6
th Central Pay Commission
(CPC) Report, at the rate of Rs.700/- per month ( i.e.10% of minimum of PB-1 + Grade pay of
Rs.1800/-) to all Central paramilitary forces personnel who are not eligible for either rent free
accommodation/House Rent Allowance (HRA). Besides, Central Para Military Forces (CPMF)
personnel have been granted ration money allowance at par with that available to the defence
personnel vide MHA order dated 24
th February, 2009. So far as desert/remote area allowance is
concerned, at present it is being paid to the BSF personnel posted in various areas of J & K and
North-Eastern States.
3.1.3 Order for grant of Risk/Hardship based allowance, i.e. High Altitude Allowance/CPMFs
personnel deployed under Ops control of Army or in areas/climate defined by Army but not under
Ops control, CPMFs deployed in LWE areas has been issued on 10 th April, 2009. The children of
BSF personnel are entitled for admission in the Kendriya Vidalayas located in any part of the
country. In the border areas of Gujarat and Rajasthan, 3 Kendriya Vidyalayas already exist and
proposal for opening of one more Kendriya Vidyalaya is under consideration of the Government.
3.1.4 The following new Kendriya Vidyalayas upto Class-V at BSF Locations have been opened
during the month of September, 2010:-

(a) Raninagar (Jalpaiguri) WB, (SHQ BSF Jalpaiguri)
(b) Humama, Srinagar (STC BSF Kashmir)
(c) Teliamura Khasiamangal, Tripura West (SHQ BSF Taliamura)
(d) Sunderbani, Jammu (SHQ BSF Sunderbani)
(e) Bhikiwind, Amritsar, Punjab
(f) Seemanagar, Krishnanagar, WB

(h) Rampur Fazilka, Punjab

Further Recommendation
3.1.5 The Ministry have stated that the desert/remote area allowance is presently paid
to the BSF personnel posted in various areas of J & K and North-Eastern States. The
Committee, however, desires that such desert/remote area allowance should be paid to
the BSF personnel in all desert/remote areas. There should not be any discrimination in
this regard. In fact, the border areas in Gujarat and Rajasthan are sparsely inhabited
having harsh climate and are non-negotiable. The personnel posted there deserve special
allowance. The committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation in this
regard.
3.1.6. The Committee has noted that there are only three Kendriya Vidyalayas in border
areas of Gujarat and Rajasthan and one is proposed to set up. Since these schools are
meant for the children of BSF personnel posted in frontier areas/border areas, they are
essential due to lack of sufficient educational infrastructure, in those places. However,
considering the large border area in Rajasthan and Gujarat, sufficient number of central
schools may be opened as per the requirement.
3.2 LOGISTICS STRATEGY FOR BORDER SURVEILLANCE AND MANAGEMENT
Recommendation
3.2.1 The Committee is of the view that that the Ministry of Home Affairs should take into

9
account the geographical and topographical location of Jaisalmer and Barmer sectors for chalking
out logistic strategy of border surveillance and management. This sector is one of the largest
having an area of 470 kms. Where BSF has been entrusted with the task of taking care of 122
BOPs and 187  gates. Since the terrain of these sectors is sandy, marred with permanent and
shifting sand dunes of varying height of 10 to 50 metres, a well chalked out strategy is the need
of the hour. Regular maintenance and repairing of roads would ensure continued surveillance of
the border areas. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry of Home Affairs should
provide a tractor to each company for regular repairing and maintenance of roads along the border
areas. The BSF should get the required basic infrastructure for monitoring the border, for example,
lateral and axial roads upto the BOPs to enhance the operational efficiency. The task of
surveillance should be carefully examined so that effective monitoring mechanism is put in place.
At present, one Battalion is entrusted on an average with the task of manning 60-62 kms. which
inhibits operational efficiency. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Home
Affairs should look into the matter at the earliest.
(Para 2.3.3 )
Action Taken
3.2.2 The holding of Tractors by sectors is as under:–
(i) Jaisalmer (S) – 08 Tractors
(ii) Jaisalmer (N) – 09 Tractors
(iii) Barmer – 09 Tractors
3.2.3 However, a case for authorization of 01 Tractor per border deployed coy for the battalions
under Jaisalmer (S), Jaisalmer (N) and Barmer Sector (Total 2 Tractors) for the purpose of regular
maintenance and repair of border roads to ensure continuous surveillance of the border area stands
submitted to the MHA.
Further Recommendation
3.2.4 The Committee takes a serious view of the fact that the Ministry has not commented
on the observations of the Committee regarding manning of 60 to 62 Kms. by one battalion
which inhibits operational efficiency. The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the
Ministry should look into the matter at the earliest. The Committee also desires to be
informed of the decisions taken regarding proposed authorization of tractors. In this
connection, the Committee also takes note of the fact that tractors, which are mainly used
for agriculture purposes may not be very suitable for Border Guarding Forces as they are
very slow. It would be better if modern, fast moving and more efficient vehicles are used
in place of tractors. Government may consider this and take necessary action in the matter.
3.3 EMERGENCY EVACUATION IN THE BHUJ/NALIYA SECTOR
Recommendation
3.3.1 The Committee observes that the existing system of emergency evacuation in the Bhuj/Naliya

10
Sector by IAF on requisition from BSF is not a proper arrangement as the helicopter has to fly
to the place of incident from Jamnagar after refuelling. The term ‘emergency evacuation’  has no
meaning as disaster will not wait for h ours before it strikes. The Committee, therefor e, recommends
that an alternative arrangement may be put in place.
(Para 2.5.2 )
Action Taken
3.3.2 This issue has been examined in the MHA. One Chetak helicopter is positioned at Jodhpur
to meet the operational requirement of BSF. The helicopter can also be utilized in case of any
disaster. With the support of Indian Air Force, the existing arrangement appears to be sufficient
to meet any emergent requirement in the area.
3.3.3 BSF MI-17 helicopters stationed at New Delhi are also deployed expeditiously for
operational or any emergency in any part of the country. The fleet of MI-17 IV, helicopters is
located at Safdarjung Airport and carrying out assigned tasks on detachment basis in the various
parts of the country.
3.3.4 Out of the 8 helicopters, 4 ALH/Dhruv are deployed in Central India, i.e. LWE affected
areas and can be redeployed at Bhuj/Naliya Sector at short notice.
Further Recommendation
3.3.5 The Committee does not agree with the contention of the Ministry of Home Affairs that the
positioning of one helicopter at Jodhpur would meet the operational requirement at short notice in
emergent situation as Gujarat Frontier has a long Border extending upto Barmer Sector. The
Government may reconsider the requirement of Helicopter in emergency situation and take strategic
decision in the matter. The Government may also consider deployment of some of the helicopters,
presently, stationed at Delhi at the strategic positions in Indo-Pak Borders of the country to meet
emergency situation.
3.4 EXPEDITIOUS CONSTRUCTION OF THE REMAINING LINK ROADS
Recommendation
3.4.1 The Committee further recommends that the construction of the remaining link roads (to the
extent of 21 kms.) be expedited. The reported wearing and tearing of the link roads from
Dharamshala to BOP Vigokot and Dharamshala to BOP Bediabet, due to heavy vehicular traffic
of NBCC/CPWD need immediate attention for repair.
(Para 2.5.4 )
Action Taken
3.4.2 The proposed works of construction of the remaining link roads have been approved by the
Competent Authority and financial releases has been made. The construction agencies, viz., Central
Public Works Department (CPWD) and National Building Construction Corporation (NBCC) have
been directed to undertake early repair of border and link roads which have been damaged due to
construction activities.

Further Recommendation
3.4.3 The Committee takes serious view of the fact that the repair of link roads is taking unduly
a long time and construction works are unnecessarily delayed, which is not acceptable. The works
may be completed within the next construction season.
3.5 STRENGTHENING OF THE MONITORING  MECHANISM IN THE BHUJ SECTOR
Recommendation
3.5.1 The Committee has been given to understand that Creek Sector is a porous border. A number
of small infiltration in collusion with anti-national elements and terrorists, enter the country
through this border. Smuggling of fake currency notes, narcotics, arms and ammunition, explosives
and trafficking of illegal immigrants, are some of the common anti-national activities that are
carried out through this area. Creek area is reportedly used as a launch pad for terrorist activities
and gathering information on patrolling pattern of the country. All these activities indicate the
nefarious design of the forces inimical to the country’ s interests, to widen the scope of terrorism
to coastal areas. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs
should immediately pay attention towards strengthening of the monitoring mechanism in the Bhuj
Sector, and plug the porous points in the border. Sooner it is done it would be in the national
interest.
(Para 2.5.5 )
Action Taken
3.5.2 In order to strengthen the monitoring mechanism in the Bhuj sector and to plug the porous
points in the border, following steps/measures have been taken:-
(i) One BSF Battalion has been exclusively deployed for the creek area
(ii) Six floating BOPs have been stationed at important check points in this area
(iii) Patrolling is being carried out with the help of speed boats and medium crafts
(iv) Two UA V and two hepter r ecee are being carried out every month
(v) Procurement of Fast Attack Crafts (FACs) : MHA has accorded procurement sanction
for US$ 81,61,799.20 (INR 38,23,80,293.00) including 10 years AIAMC (all inclusive
AMC) vide their O/o No. P- 4/869(FAC)/PC/BSF/2010/MHA (PW), dated 18.11.2010
for procurement of 4 FACs. Procurement cell, BSF has placed of tender to
M/s Tampa Yacht Manufacturing LLC, USA vice AT No. P-4/869/AT-FAC/PC/BSF/
2010/53/9259-68 dated 10.12.2010.
(vi) Procurement of Hover Crafts: MHA has sanctioned Rs.14.56 crore for procurement of
two Hover Crafts for Gujarat Frontier. Tenders were invited and subsequently same
were scarped due to non fulfilment of terms and conditions, i.e.  trial/test.
Subsequently, a decision was taken for procurement of 4-6 seater Hover Crafts
available in the range of Rs.10-30 lakhs. As desired by the CA, various firms were
contacted through e-mail for details of their product. Only two firms (M/s Neoteric
Hovercraft, INC, USA and M/s Mariah Hovercraft, Australia) have responded in this

12
regard. A Board of Officers has been detailed to conduct demonstration/trail of four
seater Hover craft at Jammu where the product of M/s Neotric Hovercraft, INC, USA
is available in India. Further action will be taken on receipt of feedback from the
Board of Officers.
Further Recommendation
3.5.3 The Committee is of the view that the tendering process may be completed at the earliest
and the Hovercraft be provided without any delay. The Committee feels that frequency of recee
by UA Vs and hepters may be increased, so that, more vigil can be kept in this porous border area,
effectively.

Recommendation
3.6.1 The Committee also urges upon the Ministry for an early decision on construction of
Forward Command Post.
(Para 3.10.3 )
Action Taken
3.6.2 BSF has asked its field formations to forward a detailed proposal for creation of forward
command post in addition to already existing Observation Posts, steel towers and naka machans

3.6.3 The Committee observes that no tangible progress has been made in regard to

more persons to witness the retreat ceremony as the existing one can accommodate small number

coupled with the time taken to move the victims to hospital located far off from the border.

formation.
14

15
4.3 UPGRADING INDIA’S BORDER SURVEILLANCE AND MILITARY PREPAREDNESS
Recommendation
4.3.1 The Committee was apprised that the bund which was constructed in order to provide
security cover to the persons engaged in fencing work, had now become counterproductive and
was helping militants. It has been reported that Pakistan has made a lot of construction after
ceasefire. It had constructed 97  OP Towers and 162 barracks. The Committee, therefore, strongly
feels that Government of India should upgrade India’s border surveillance and military
preparedness.
(Para 3.2.1 )
Action Taken
4.3.2 A proposal for construction of earthen bundh on home side of fencing, naka cum machan
cum fighting bunkers and road in Jammu stands submitted to MHA. The proposal was discussed
in 19th HLEC held on 13 January, 2009 and the same is under active consideration for CCS
approval.
4.4 REPLACEMENT OF THE EXISTING BORDER FLOODLIGHT (BFL) SYSTEM
Recommendation
4.4.1 Keeping in view the fact that the floodlight equipments have outlived their life and cables
have also become obsolete and damaged, the Committee recommends that it is necessary to replace
the existing Border Flood Light (BFL) system with utmost expedition.
(Para 3.4.1 )
Action Taken
4.4.2 The Government is aware that the floodlight equipments along Indo-Pakistan border
including Punjab sector have outlived their life and cables have also become obsolete and damaged
since these floodlights were erected long back. A proposal regarding upgradation/replacement of the
existing Border Flood Lights system in Punjab sector with new and more illuminating devices is
under examination of the Government.
4.5 REALIGNING THE FENCE TOWARDS THE ZERO LINE
Recommendation
4.5.1 The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs should take up the issue of
realigning the fence towards the zero line on top priority as large tracks of cultivable lands lie
beyond the present fencing area. The Committee also recommends that shifting of fencing in
Abohar and Ferozpur Sectors be completed in a scheduled time frame and the proposal of shifting
of fencing in Gurudaspur Sector be finalized and approved at the earliest.
(Para 3.6.1 )
Action Taken
4.5.2 Realignment of the fence towards the zero line, due to large tracks of cultivable land lying
ahead of the present fencing alignment, has been considered by the Government. A proposal for
forward shifting of 23.380 km. of fencing closer to zero line in Ferozpur sector has been approved
by Government in January 2008 and works are in progress.

16
4.6 CONSTRUCTION OF A PONTOON BRIDGE
Recommendation
4.6.1 The committee appreciates the hardships being faced by farmers in cultivating their land
beyond the rivers Tarna, Sutlej and Ravi. The committee, therefore, recommends that government
should explore the possibility of construction of a pontoon bridge at Chakri over river Tarna,
bridge over Ravi at Kakkar village and a bridge over Sutlej.
(Para 3.8.1 )
Action Taken
4.6.2 BSF has earmarked some locations where construction of bridges/culverts over the rivers
in Punjab needs to be taken. Operational clearance from Ministry of Defence is being obtained
before finalizing the proposal and obtaining necessary approvals.
4.7 CONSTRUCTION OF PUCCA ROADS ALONG THE ENTIRE STRETCH OF PUNJAB
FRONTIER
Recommendation
4.7.1 The Committee expresses its serious concern over the absence of Black Top (Pucca) road
along the entire stretch of fencing of Punjab Frontier. The Committee would like the Ministry of
Home Affairs to look into this grey area and examine the possibility of construction of pucca roads
along the entire stretch of Punjab Frontier. The Committee strongly recommends that axial and
lateral roads connecting border fence gates, are required to be constructed for effective patrolling
of the border areas. The Committee is of the strong view that pontoon bridges/belley bridges are
also required to be constructed at strategic locations to facilitate movement of BSF troops as well
as farmers. The Committee further recommends that the construction of pucca roads and their
timely repairing would improve better surveillance of border areas by the BSF and curbing of
infiltration from other side of the border area.
(Para 3.10.1 )
Action Taken
4.7.2 A proposal for construction of 394 km. of lateral and 210 km. of axial roads in Punjab is
under examination in the Ministry of Home Affairs.
4.7.3 Regarding construction of pontoon bridges on rivers for accessibility during the fair
weather, need based bridges are constructed on strategic locations every year.

17
OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSION/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE —
AT A GLANCE
EXPEDITIOUS APPROVAL OF REVISED COST
The Committee desires that the construction work of fencing, road, floodlighting and
Border Outposts in Gujarat Sector may be completed as per schedule. (Para 1.1.3)
COMPLETION OF THE CONSTRUCTION OF BORDER ROADS WITHOUT FURTHER
DELAY
The Committee recommends that the work in progress may be completed at the
earliest. The balance pending works may be taken up and completed as per targets without
time and cost overruns. (Para 1.2.4 )
REALIGNING THE FENCE TOWARDS THE ZERO LINE
The Committee recommends that there should not be any delay in the completion of
the project on shifting of 23, 380 Kms. of fencing closur e to Zero Line in Ferozpur Sector.
The Committee desires to be informed of the time-frame by when the work will be
completed. (Para 1.3.3)
ONE MORE BATTALION AT THE FEROZPUR SECTOR
The Committee desires that Ferozpur Sector may be included among the key
locations plans. (Para 1.6.3)
STELLAR ROLE OF BSF IN GUARDING THE COUNTRY'S FRONTIERS
The Ministry have stated that the desert/remote area allowance is presently paid to
the BSF personnel posted in various areas of J&K and North-Eastern States. The
Committee, however, desires that such desert/remote area allowance should be paid to the
BSF personnel in all desert/remote areas. There should not be any discrimination in this
regard. In fact, the border areas in Gujarat and Rajasthan are sparsely inhabited having
harsh climate and are non-negotiable. The personnel posted there deserve special allowance.
The committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation in this regard.
(Para 3.1.5)
The Committee has noted that there are only three Kendriya Vidyalayas in border
areas of Gujarat and Rajasthan and one is proposed to set up. Since these schools are
meant for the children of BSF personnel posted in frontier areas/border areas, they are
essential due to lack of sufficient educational infrastructure, in those places. However,
considering the large border area in Rajasthan and Gujarat, sufficient number of central
schools may be opened as per the requirement. (Para 3.1.6)
17

18
LOGISTICS STRATEGY FOR BORDER SURVEILLANCE AND MANAGEMENT
The Committee takes a serious view of the fact that the Ministry has not commented
on the observations of the Committee regarding manning of 60 to 62 Kms. by one battalion
which inhibits operational efficiency. The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the
Ministry should look into the matter at the earliest. The Committee also desires to be
informed of the decisions taken regarding proposed authorization of tractors. In this
connection, the Committee also takes note of the fact that tractors, which are mainly used
for agriculture purposes may not be very suitable for Border Guarding Forces as they are
very slow. It would be better if modern, fast moving and more efficient vehicles are used
in place of tractors. Government may consider this and take necessary action in the matter.
(Para 3.2.4)
EMERGENCY EVACUATION IN THE BHUJ/NALIYA SECTOR
The Committee does not agree with the contention of the Ministry of Home Affairs
that the positioning of one helicopter at Jodhpur would meet the operational requirement
at short notice in emergent situation as Gujarat Frontier has a long Border extending upto
Barmer Sector. The Government may reconsider the requirement of Helicopter in
emergency situation and take strategic decision in the matter. The Government may also
consider deployment of some of the helicopters, presently, stationed at Delhi at the strategic
positions in Indo-Pak Borders of the country to meet emergency situation. (Para 3.3.5)
EXPEDITIOUS CONSTRUCTION OF THE REMAINING LINK ROADS
The Committee takes serious view of the fact that the repair of link roads is
taking unduly a long time and construction works are unnecessarily delayed, which is
not acceptable. The works may be completed within the next construction season.
(Para 3.4.3)
STRENGTHENING OF THE MONITORING MECHANISM IN THE BHUJ SECTOR
The Committee is of the view that the tendering process may be completed at the
earliest and the Hovercraft be provided without any delay. The Committee feels that
frequency of recee by UA Vs and hepters may be increased, so that, more vigil can be kept
in this porous border area, effectively. (Para 3.5.3)
CONSTRUCTION OF FORWARD COMMAND POST
The Committee observes that no tangible progress has been made in regard to the
construction of Forward Command Post despite the recommendation made by it in 2008. The
Committee during study visits, noticed the necessity of construction of forward command
post. The Committee, therefore, feels that the issue of Forward Command Post is
strategically very important. An early decision may, therefore, be taken in the matter.
(Para 3.6.3)
UPGRADING AMENITIES FOR THE TOURISTS
The Committee observes that nothing has been mentioned about the Action Taken

matter. The Committee also recommends that developmental work at Retreat Point at
Hussainiwala be completed within the stipulated time-frame and without cost overrun in
order to facilitate the visitors. (Para 3.7.3)

1
REPORT
CHAPTER-I
BACKGROUND
1.0 According to Statements of Objects and Reasons of the Border Security Force
(Amendment) Bill, 2011, the Bill proposes to amend the long title, Section 4 and 139 of the Border
Security Force Act, 1968 to enable the Central Government to deploy the BSF in areas other than
the borders of India or its adjoining areas i.e. hinterland areas for internal security as well.
1.1.1 The Ministry of Home Affairs in the background note stated that the Border Security Force
was raised as an Armed Force of the Union in 1965 for ensuring the security of the Borders of
India and for matters connected therewith. The Border Security Force Act, 1968 was enacted to
provide for the constitution and regulation of an Armed Force of the Union for ensuring the
security of the borders of India and for matters connected therewith. Under Rule 15 of the BSF
Rules, 1969, the BSF has been assigned following tasks while deployed along the borders:–
(i) Promote a sense of security among the people living in the border area.
(ii) Prevent trans-border crimes, un-authorised entry into or exit from the territory of
India.
(iii) Prevent smuggling and any other illegal activity.
1.1.2 The Ministry stated that as on date, the Central Government has given powers to the BSF
personnel in border areas under the Customs Act, the Passport Act, the NDPS Act and the CrPC
by way of issuing suitable notifications under the respective legislations. These powers, so
conferred, primarily relate to arrest, search and seizure within the prescribed border belt, which
is 80 kms. in the State of Gujarat, 50 kms. in the State of Rajasthan and 15 kms. in the States
of West Bengal, Assam and Punjab.  No such limit has been prescribed in the case of J&K and
five North Eastern States viz., Meghalaya, Nagaland, Mizoram, Tripura and Manipur.
1.1.3 The Ministry of Home Affairs in its background note apprised the Committee that in the
recent times, apart from safeguarding the borders of the country (primarily with Pakistan and
Bangladesh), the BSF has acquired country wide presence as it has been assigned multifarious roles
and responsibilities in different parts of the country. A large segment of the force is deployed in
North-East, J&K for handling counter insurgency/anti-militancy operations and in the naxal affected
states like Chhattisgarh, Orissa etc. Besides, BSF is also extensively used during elections,
communal riots and other law and order duties including the natural calamities in various States,
in aid of civil authorities.
1.1.4 The Ministry of Home Affairs also apprised the Committee that recently, the BSF personnel
posted in the hinterland are facing certain limitations as to their effectiveness in aiding the State
Governments because of the fact that they cannot exercise the powers of arrest, search and seizure
under the CrPC in the absence of necessary legislation. While considering conferring of necessary
powers of search, seizure and arrest in the hinterland under the provisions of CrPC, Ministry of
Law and Justice was consulted by the Ministry of Home Affairs. Ministry of Law and Justice,
while furnishing their opinion on the matter had stated that powers under Sections 41 (1), 46, 47,
48, 49, 51 (1), 52, 53, 74, 100, 102, 129, 149, 150, 151 and 152 of CrPC cannot be given to
the BSF personnel in the hinterland unless Sections 4 and 139 of the BSF Act, 1968 are suitably
amended.

2
1.2 Section 4 of the BSF Act, 1968 reads as under:–
“4.(1) There shall be an armed force of the Union called the Border Security Force for
ensuring the security of the borders of India.
(2) Subject to provisions of this Act, the Force shall be constituted in such manner
as may be prescribed and the conditions of service of the members of the Force
shall be such as may be prescribed.”
1.3 Section 139 of the BSF Act, 1968 was incorporated in the BSF Act, 1968 as an enabling
provision which provides that-
“The Central Govt. may, by general or special order published in the Official Gazette direct
that, subject to such conditions and limitations, and within the local limits of such area
adjoining the borders of India , as may be specified in the order, any member of the Force
may:
(i) for the purpose of prevention of any offence punishable under the Passport
(Entry into India) Act, 1920, the Registration of Foreigners Act, 1939, the
Central Excise and Salt Act, 1944, the Foreigners Act, 1946, the Foreign
Exchange Regulation Act, 1947, the Customs Act, 1962 or the Passports
Act, 1967 or of any cognizable offence punishable under any other Central Act;
or
(ii) for the purpose of apprehending any person who has committed any offence
referred to in clause (i), exercise or discharge such of the powers or duties under
that Act or any other Central Act as may be specified in the said order, being
the powers and duties which, in the opinion of the Central Government, an
officer of the corresponding or lower rank is by that or such other Act
empowered to exercise or discharge for the said purposes”.
1.4 The Ministry of Home Affairs pointed out that though BSF has been used in the recent past
for various eventualities, Section 4 restricts the role of BSF to ensure the security of the borders
of India.  Therefore, in order to deploy the BSF in any part of the country for any emergent duties,
this Section needs to be amended for the effective utilization of the service of BSF in the hinterland
as well.
1.5 The Ministry of Home Affairs further stated that Section 4 and 139 of the BSF Act have
a close inter-relationship and both these sections were initially formulated to suit the requirement
of the Force in border areas.  During the enactment of the Act, the legislation, probably could not
foresee a situation where the BSF may have to be used for duties, other than those related to
security of borders of India. Presently, due to legal constraints, the State Governments on whose
request the BSF is deployed for maintenance of law and order, often find it not so effective, except
being of psychological value, in view of the fact that the personnel so deployed do not have the
necessary powers of search, seizure and arrest.  The Ministry felt that in the coming times, the
deployment of BSF personnel in the hinterland for fighting the menace of naxalism and terrorism
as also during elections and rioting, etc, is likely to increase and it is absolutely necessary that
suitable enabling provisions may be incorporated in the present BSF Act so that the force can be
put to best use in an effective manner without any legal complication in the absence of such
power.
1.6 Accordingly, following suitable amendments in Sections 4 and 139 of the Border
Security Force Act, 1968 have been proposed through the Border Security Force (Amendment)
Bill, 2011

3
(i) Section 4 (1) would read as under : “ There shall be an armed force of the Union called
the Border Security Force for ensuring the security of the borders of India and performing
such other duties as may be entrusted to it by the Central Government .”
(ii) Section 139 (1) would read as under : “The Central Govt. may, by general or special
order published in the Official Gazette direct that, subject to such conditions and
limitations, as may be specified in the order, any member of the Force may:–
(i) for the purpose of prevention of any offence punishable under the Passport (Entry
into India) Act, 1920, the Registration of Foreigners Act, 1939, the Central Excise
Act, 1944, the Foreigners Act, 1946, the Foreign Exchange Management
Act, 1999, the Customs Act, 1962 or the Passports Act, 1967 or of any cognizable
offence punishable under any other Central Act; or
1.7 The Ministry of Home Affairs argued that proposed amendment in section 139(1) is
consequential in nature as the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944 has since been renamed as the
Central Excise Act, 1944 and the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947 has since been replaced
by the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999.
1.8 Justifying the proposed amendment in sections 4 and 139 the Ministry of Home Affairs
stated that similar provisions already exist in Sections 4 and 154 of the ITBP Act, 1992 and
Sections 4 and 153 of the SSB Act, 2007 as these Acts were formulated in recent times. The
Ministry also stated that as regards the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), Section 16 of the
CRPF Act, 1949 enables that the Central Government to confer or impose upon any member of
the force any of the powers or duties conferred or imposed on a police officer of any class or
grade by any law for the time being in force. Accordingly, vide Notification No.S.O.2821 dated
27
th July, 1976. The CRPF personnel have been empowered to exercise the powers of a Police
Officer under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 anywhere in the Country wherever they are
called upon to perform their duties. The Ministry therefore stated that considering the legal
constraints and the difficulties being faced by the State Governments as well as the Central
Government in proper utilization of the BSF in the hinterland, suitable amendments in Sections 4
and 139 of the BSF Act have been proposed.

4
4
CHAPTER-II
PRESENTATION OF MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS
2.0 The Committee in its sitting held on 23 rd September, 2011, heard the Home Secretary on the
Border Security Force (Amendment) Bill, 2011. The Secretary (Internal Security), Ministry of
Home Affairs made presentation on the Bill.  Further explaining about the need for change in the
BSF Act, 1968, it was stated in the presentation that  there had been significant changes in the
nature of duties of BSF over a period of time from purely a border guarding force to other
important additional duties like, Counter Insurgency, Internal Security, Anti-Militancy and Anti-Naxal
Operations in North-East, J&K and LWE Affected Areas/ States, Deployment during Parliamentary
and Assembly Elections. States also requested for Panchayat Elections, assisting the State
Governments in aid to civil authorities for maintenance of Law and Order during internal
disturbances including communal riots etc, assisting the State Governments during Natural
calamities/disasters in different parts of the Country.
2.1 Outlining the limitation of the Present Provisions, he stated that the powers given under the
legislations like Cr.PC, etc. can be exercised only within the prescribed border belt, i.e. 80 kms.
in the State of Gujarat, 50 kms. in the State of Rajasthan, 15 kms. in the States of West Bengal,
Assam and Punjab. No powers, however, exist  in the States such as Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand,
Odisha, Haryana, Karnataka, Kerala etc. though BSF personnel are deployed in the hinterland for
Counter Insurgency, Internal Security (IS) and Anti-Naxal Operations, Elections duties, etc. He
further stated that no powers can be conferred in the Hinterland in the absence of the enabling
provisions  under the Act.
2.2 Giving further Justification for amendments brought in the Act, the Secretary (IS), in his
presentation made the following submissions:–
• The State Governments, on whose request the BSF is deployed are not able to use the
force effectively as the BSF personnel so deployed do not have the requisite basic
powers of search, seizure and arrest in the hinterland.
• In the absence of powers, deployment of BSF personnel is only of a psychological value.
• Such amendment shall further enable the Central Government to issue necessary
notifications by virtue of which powers can be bestowed on BSF in areas other than
Border areas
• Like the BSF, ITBP (Indo-Tibetan Border Police Force) and the SSB (Sashastra Seema
Bal) are also the Border Guarding Forces deployed on the Indo-China and Indo-Nepal
Borders respectively and performing additional roles in the hinterland.
• Provisions bestowing powers on CRPF on similar lines already exist under Section 16
of the CRPF Act, 1949 and the CRPF personnel vide Notification dated 27
th July, 1976
have been given powers of a Police Officer under the CrPC,  1973, wherever they are
called upon to perform duties.
• Such an enabling provision would permit the deployment of BSF personnel for internal
security duties in the hinterland and will allow the Government to empower them
appropriately to perform their duties.

5
• Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944 has been renamed as Central Excise Act, 1944.
• Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947 has been amended and renamed as Foreign
Exchange Management Act, 1999.
